bitterness.e: From Middle English bitternesse, biternesse, from Old English biternes (“bitterness; grief”), equivalent to bitter + -ness.

insolent.e: PIE word *swé From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin īnsolēns (“unaccustomed, unwanted, unusual, immoderate, excessive, arrogant, insolent”), from in- (privative prefix) + solēns, present participle of solēre…

circular.e: From Middle English circuler, circuleer, circulere, from Old French circulier (French circulaire), from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (“ring”). By surface analysis, circle + -ar.

purge.e: From Middle English purgen, from Old French purgier, from Latin pūrgō (“to make pure, to cleanse”), from pūrus (“clean, pure”) + agō (“to make, to do”). The slang sense derived via the 2013 film The Purge.

mingle.e: From earlier mingil, mengle, from Middle English menglen, equivalent to ming + -le. Cognate with Dutch mengelen (“to mingle, mix”), German mengen (“to mingle, mix”). More at ming.

casually.e: From Middle English casually, casuelly, casuali, casuely, equivalent to casual + -ly.

handler.e: From Middle English handler, handiller, equivalent to handle + -er.

hobbs.e: From a medieval diminutive form of the given name Robert + the patronymic suffix -s.

ph.d..e: , an abbreviation of Philosophiae Doctor (“Doctor of Philosophy”).

multiply.e: From Old French multiplier, from Latin multiplicō, from multi (“many”) + plicō (“to fold”). The noun presumably derives from the verb.

confinement.e: Borrowed from French confinement. By surface analysis, confine + -ment.

divert.e: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

alfonso.e: From Spanish Alfonso and Italian Alfonso. Doublet of Alphonse.

ambrose.e: From Latin saints' name Ambrosius, from Ancient Greek ἀμβρόσιος (ambrósios, “immortal, divine”). Compare Athanasius.

adriana.e: From Latin Adriāna. By surface analysis, Adrian + -a. Doublet of Adrienne and Adrian.

gunther.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰéntis Proto-Germanic *gunþiz Proto-Indo-European *ker-der.

lawful.e: From Middle English laweful, equivalent to law + -ful, conflated with Middle English leful, leeful, leveful (“according to law, lawful, pertaining to law”). See also leveful.

damian.e: From the Ancient Greek name Δαμιανός (Damianós) which was derived from δαμάω (damáō, “to tame”) (see δαμάζω (damázō)). Name known in Ancient Greece, later borne by Christian saints.

reasonably.e: From Middle English resonably, equivalent to reasonable + -ly. Piecewise doublet of rationably.

suzuki.e: Borrowed from Japanese Suzuki (Suzuki), from Japanese すずき (Suzuki, “surname”) or Japanese スズキ (Suzuki, “automaker”); from Japanese 鈴木 (Suzuki) (automaker from the surname).

myra.e: First used by the poet Fulke Greville, possibly as an anagram of Mary.

mainstream.e: From main + stream. Cognate with Icelandic meginstraumur (“a main current, mainstream”).

sykes.e: From Middle English sike (“marshy stream, gutter, ditch”).

alimony.e: Known since the 17th century, from Latin alimōnia (“food, support, nourishment, sustenance”) (English aliment, as in alimentary), itself from alō (“to nourish”) + -mōnia (“action, state, condition”).

budapest.e: Borrowed from Hungarian Budapest, from Buda + Pest.

ore.e: From Middle English or, oor, blend of Old English ōra (“ore, unwrought metal”), of uncertain origin, and ār (“brass, copper, bronze”), from Proto-West Germanic *aiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *aiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h…

curl.e: From metathesis of Middle English crulle (“curled, curly”), of uncertain origin but probably from an unrecorded Old English word or from Middle Dutch crul, crulle (“curl”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent…

cabaret.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em-der. Proto-Indo-Iranian *kmáratider. Proto-Iranian *kamarāder. Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára)bor. Latin camerader. Old Northern French cambereteder.

manufacturer.e: Etymology tree English manufacture Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

boulder.e: From late Middle English bulder, short for Middle English bulder ston (“a stone that's been worn into a round shape, boulder, cobblestone”), possibly from Old Swedish *buldersten, itself possibly from Old Swedish bulder…

mush.e: Probably a variant of mash, or from a dialectal variant of Middle English mos (“mush, pulp, porridge”); compare Middle English appelmos (“applesauce”), from Old English mōs (“food, victuals, porridge, mush”), from Proto…

recycle.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-redup.

disarm.e: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.

elusive.e: From Latin elusus, past participle of eludo (“to parry a blow, to deceive”).

snarl.e: From Middle English snarlen, frequentative of snaren (“to trap, tangle”). Equivalent to snare + -le.

chiu.e: From several different Chinese surnames, including: * Cantonese 趙 /赵 (ziu⁶) * Hokkien 周 (Chiu) * Mandarin 邱 (Qiū), Wade–Giles romanization: Chʻiu¹. Doublet of Qiu.

harmful.e: From Middle English harmful, from Old English *hearmful (suggested by hearmfullīċ (“harmful; hurtful”)), equivalent to harm + -ful. Cognate with German harmvoll, Danish harmfuld, Swedish harmfull.

horseback.e: From Middle English horsebacke, horsebak, horsbak, equivalent to horse + back.

helene.e: From French Hélène and from German Helene. Doublet of Helen, Helena, and Elaine.

thankfully.e: From Middle English thankfully, thankefully, þonkfulliche, from Old English þancfullīċe, equivalent to thankful + -ly.

recreate.e: From Middle English recreate, from the participle stem of Latin recreāre (“to restore”), from re- (“re-”) + creāre (“to create”).

navigate.e: First attested in 1588; borrowed from Latin nāvigātus, the perfect passive participle of nāvigō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from nāvis (“ship”) + -igō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us (“boat”).

pun.e: From Middle English ponnen, ponen, punen, from Old English punian, pūnian (“to pound, beat, bray, bruise, crush, grind”), from Proto-Germanic *punōną (“to break to pieces, pulverize”). See pound.

ethnic.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *swé Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *swe-dʰh₁- Proto-Hellenic *séswōtʰa Ancient Greek ἔθω (éthō) Proto-Indo-European *-nós Ancient Greek -νος (-nos) ?

esteem.e: First at end of 16th century; borrowed from Middle French estimer, borrowed from Latin aestimō. See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.

duffy.e: From the Irish surname, from Ó Dubhthaigh (literally “descendant of Dubhthach”) and Mac Duibhshíthe (literally “son of Duibhshíth”), from dubh (“black”) + sìth (“peace”), comparable to the surname Duff.

triad.e: PIE word *tréyes From Latin triad-, stem of trias (“three, triad”), from Ancient Greek τριάς (triás). By surface analysis, tri- + -ad.

iraqi.e: Borrowed from Arabic عِرَاقِيّ (ʕirāqiyy, “Iraqi”), equivalent to Iraq + -i.

portfolio.e: From Italian portafoglio; cognate with French portefeuille (“folder, wallet”), from Latin portāre (“to carry”) and folium (“sheet”). The meaning "collection of responsibilities" came by extension in the 1930s.

booby.e: 17th century. From Spanish bobo, from Latin balbus (“stammering”). (bird): Compare typologically Translingual Morus, German Tölpel, Polish głuptak (akin to głupek), Russian о́луша (óluša) (akin to о́лух (ólux)).

simms.e: From Sim, the short form of Simon + -s.

racism.e: Borrowed from French racisme, equivalent to race + -ism.

mayo.e: The name of the village and county in Ireland is from Irish Maigh Eo (“plain of yew trees”).

stingy.e: Uncertain, possibly from stinge, a dialectal variation of sting (verb).

kaiser.e: Inherited from Middle English kayser, from Old High German keisar (“emperor”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaisar, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar.

registry.e: a bookmark”), partly from Medieval Latin regesterium, registerium and probably also partly formed with -ery. Equivalent to register + -y.

shah.e: Borrowed from Persian شاه (šâh), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (šāh), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/). Doublet of check. More at chess.

duo.e: PIE word *dwóh₁ From French duo or Italian duo, from Latin duo (“two”), from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Doublet of two, which was inherited via Proto-Germanic.

gymnastics.e: From gymnastic: see -ics; from Latin gymnasticus, from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gumnastikós), from γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “athlete, gymnast”), from γῠμνᾰ́ζω (gŭmnắzō, “to train, exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”…

jag.e: The noun is from late Middle English jagge, from Old English giagga, giacga.

bernadette.e: From French Bernadette, made famous by St. Bernadette of Lourdes.

valiant.e: From Middle English vailaunt (“having or showing courage or valour, valiant; characterized by valour; powerful, strong; person of valour or strength; excellent, worthy; beneficial, useful; valuable; legally valid, bindi…

attachment.e: From French attachement. By surface analysis, attach + -ment.

trans.e: Learned borrowing from Latin trāns (“on the other side of”). Doublet of très.

mega.e: From the prefix mega-, from Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great, large, mighty”).

crispy.e: From Middle English crispy (“crisped, curly”), equivalent to crisp + -y.

qu.e: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of the Mandarin 區 /区.

persuasive.e: From Middle French persuasif, from Medieval Latin persuāsīvus, from Latin past participle stem of persuādēre + -īvus.

turmoil.e: Unknown. First appears c. 1526. Perhaps from Old French tremouille (“the hopper of a mill”).

shoving.e: From Middle English schovynge; equivalent to shove + -ing.

unworthy.e: From Middle English unworthy, equivalent to un- + worthy.

ronny.e: Shortening of Ronald + -y. A less common spelling of Ronnie.

rooting.e: From Middle English rotynge (“rooting”); equivalent to root + -ing.

irma.e: From German Irma in the nineteenth century. Short form of Germanic names beginning with irm(en)-, erm(en) "whole, entire", from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz. Cognate with English Emma.

mcqueen.e: " See McSweeney. * Also as a Scottish and Irish surname, from Mac Shuain, based on Old Norse sveinn (“boy servant”). Also compare Swain, McSwan.

stoop.e: From Middle English stoupen, from Old English stūpian (“to bow, bend”), from Proto-West Germanic *stūpōn, from Proto-Germanic *stūpōną, *stūpijaną (“to stand out”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewb- (“to push, butt, kn…

volleyball.e: Etymology tree English volley Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-der. Proto-Germanic *balluz Old English *beall Middle English bal English ball English volleyball From volley + ball.

chord.e: Variant of cord, with spelling alteration due to Latin chorda (“cord”), ultimately from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”). No relation to French accord (“chord”) and its derivations.

berkeley.e: From Old English beorc (“birch”) + leah (“meadow, leigh”). Equivalent to birch + -ley (“lea”).

radiant.e: From Middle English radyant, from Latin radiāns, radiantis, present participle of radiāre (“to emit rays or beams”).

anticipation.e: From Middle English anticipacioun, from Middle French anticipation and its etymon Latin anticipātiō, anticipātiōnem. By surface analysis, anticipate + -ion.

dalek.e: Coined by Terry Nation in 1963 for his script of The Mutants (later retitled "The Daleks"), the second serial of the first season of Doctor Who. Accounts of how he devised the word vary.

arouse.e: Etymology tree English a- Middle English rousen English rouse English arouse From a- + rouse.

paralysis.e: Borrowed from Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis, “palsy”), from παραλύω (paralúō, “to disable on one side”). By surface analysis, para- + -lysis. Doublet of palsy.

ferocious.e: Taken from Latin ferōx (“wild, bold, savage, fierce”) + -ous.

heinous.e: From Middle English heynous, from Anglo-Norman hainous, heinous (compare French haineux) from Old French haïr, hadir (“to hate”) (compare Old French en-hadir (“to become filled with hate”)), from Frankish *hattjan (“to…

roulette.e: Borrowed from French roulette (“roulette, little wheel”). The sense "situation with a random chance of incurring serious harm" may be abstracted from Russian roulette.

olaf.e: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *anô Proto-Germanic *laibō Proto-Germanic *Anulaibaz Proto-Norse *ᚨᚾᚢᛚᚨᛁᛒᚨᛉ (*anulaibaʀ) Old Norse Óláfrder. English Olaf Derived from Old Norse Óláfr.

enjoyable.e: Etymology tree English enjoy Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor. Middle English -able English -able English enjoyable From enjoy + -able.

torso.e: From Italian torso, from Late Latin tursus, from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos, “Bacchic staff”). Doublet of thyrse, thyrsus, and torse.

compassionate.e: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“to feel sorry for”). By surface analysis, compassion + -ate.

delegation.e: Borrowed from Latin dēlēgātiō, dēlēgātiōnis, from dēlēgō: compare French délégation.

plaque.e: Unadapted borrowing from French plaque (“plate, sheet (of metal); slab (of marble); bacteria on teeth”), from French plaquer, Middle French plaquer (“to plate”), from Middle Dutch placken (“to patch, beat metal into a t…

bowman.e: From Middle English boweman, bouman, boughman, equivalent to bow + -man.

uterus.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úd Proto-Indo-European *-teros Proto-Indo-European *úderos Latin uteruslbor. English uterus Learned borrowing from Latin uterus.

kristina.e: A modern Scandinavian spelling variant of Christina

neigh.e: Inherited from Middle English neyen, from Old English hnǣġan, from Proto-West Germanic *hnaijan, from Proto-Germanic *hnajjaną (“to neigh”).

tibet.e: Of unclear origin, but probably from Old Turkic 𐱅𐰇𐰯𐰇𐱅 (Töpüt) ('hilly, mountainous place') via Classical Persian تبت (tabbat, tubbat).

fez.e: From Ottoman Turkish فس (fes) (modern Turkish fes), named after Fez, Morocco, (capital of the Kingdom of Morocco until 1927), where the dye to color the hat was extracted from crimson berries.

charcoal.e: From Middle English charcole, from charren (“to change, turn”) + cole (“coal”), from Old English cierran (“to change, turn”) + col (“coal”). By surface analysis, char (Etymology 3 [verb]) + coal.

healer.e: From Middle English helere, the agent noun of heal; analysed as heal + -er. Cognate with Dutch heler (“healer”), German Heiler (“healer”), Icelandic heilari (“healer”).

eel.e: From Middle English el (“eel”), from Old English ǣl (“eel”), from Proto-West Germanic *āl (“eel”), from Proto-Germanic *ēlaz (“eel”), which is of unknown origin.

tamil.e: Etymology tree Old Tamil 𑀢𑀫𑀺𑀵𑁰 (tamiḻ) Tamil தமிழ் (tamiḻ)bor. English Tamil Borrowed from Tamil தமிழ் (tamiḻ, “Tamil”); see that entry for theories.

naw.e: In Scottish use, from Scots naw, naa, na, from Middle English na, from Old English nā (“no, never”). More generally, a colloquial, unarticulated form of no; compare nah. More at no.

camouflage.e: Etymology tree French camoufler Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-tós Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos Proto-Italic *-ātos Latin -ātus Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos La…

seagulls.e: From seagull, from the Brighton & Hove Albion logo having a seagull.

seagull.e: From sea + gull. The second element is from a Brythonic language. Compare Welsh gwylan, Breton gouelan.

hub.e: From earlier hubbe, which has the same immediate origin as hob. Hub was originally a dialectal word; its ultimate origin is unknown.

buckley.e: From Old English bucca (“he-goat”) + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”). Equivalent to buck + -ley (“lea”).

furry.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-der. Proto-Germanic *fōdrą Frankish *fōdrbor. Anglo-Norman fuerrebor.

pronto.e: Borrowed from Spanish pronto, from Latin prōmptus. Doublet of prompt.

sedan.e: The sense of "windowed chair" was first used by Sir Sanders Duncombe in 1634, possibly from a southern Italian dialect of Italian sede (“seat”), from Latin sedes.

kermit.e: Variant of English and Manx Kermode, cognate with Irish Mac Diarmata and Scots Gaelic McDiarmid (“son of Dermot”). Popularized in the US by the naming of Kermit Roosevelt (after a Manx ancestor).

amir.e: From Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander, prince”). Doublet of amir, emir, admiral, and amira.

emir.e: From Middle French emir, from Ottoman Turkish امیر (emir), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander, prince”). Doublet of amir, Amir, admiral, and amira.

edible.e: From Late Latin edibilis, from Latin edō (“eat”). Doublet of eatable.

trifle.e: From Middle English trifle, trifel, triful, trefle, truyfle, trufful, from Old French trufle (“mockery”), a byform of trufe, truffe (“deception”), of uncertain origin.

calcutta.e: Anglicization of Bengali কলকাতা (kolkata), which is now rendered Kolkata. Unrelated to English Calicut.

crotch.e: Of disputed origin; two possibilities seem likely: * From Middle English croche, variant of crucche (“crutch”); compare crook. * From Middle English croche, variant of crouche (“cross, crozier”).

tariq.e: Borrowed from Arabic طَارِق (ṭāriq, “messenger, nocturnal visitor, or morning star”), from طَرَقَ (ṭaraqa, “to knock, to rap”).

leila.e: From Arabic لَيْلَى (laylā). Taken into English usage through nineteenth-century literature.

snail.e: From Middle English snayl, snail, from the Old English sneġel, from Proto-Germanic *snagilaz. Cognate with Low German Snagel, Snâel, Snâl (“snail”), German Schnegel (“slug”).

ursula.e: From Latin Ursula, the name of a fourth century saint. Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos cognate with Arcady.

vista.e: Borrowed from Italian vista (“view, sight”), from visto, past participle of vedere (“to see”), from Latin vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision, video, visa.

sorta.e: A written form of a reduction of sort of.

fiend.e: From Middle English fend, feend (“enemy; demon”), from Old English fēond (“enemy”), Proto-West Germanic *fijand, from Proto-Germanic *fijandz.

ultra.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Latin ūls Proto-Indo-European *-teros? Latin -ter Old Latin -ād Latin -ā Latin ultrābor. English ultra From Latin ultra.

pinkie.e: From Dutch pinkje (literally “little finger”), which in the Holland dialects takes the form pinkie.

voluntary.e: From Middle English voluntarie, from Old French volontaire, from Latin voluntārius (“willing, of free will”), from voluntās (“will, choice, desire”), from volēns, present participle of volo (“to will”).

widely.e: From Middle English wijdly, equivalent to wide + -ly.

uncommon.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-West Germanic *un- Old English un- Middle English un- English un- English common English uncommon From un- + common.

blacky.e: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *blakaz Proto-West Germanic *blak Old English blæc Middle English blak English black Proto-Germanic *-j-, *-ij- Proto-West Germanic *-i, *-ī Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y Eng…

infiltrate.e: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.

erika.e: Spelling variant of Erica, the feminine form of Eric, or borrowed directly from modern Scandinavia, ultimately from Old Norse Eiríkr.

sophomore.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós) Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō Ancient Greek -ίζω (-ízō) Ancient Greek σοφίζω (sophízō) Proto-Indo…

ringo.e: From ring + -o. From the stage name of one of the Beatles, Ringo Starr, actually named Richard Starkey, the drummer of the quartet. From ring, from the rings worn by Richard "Ringo Starr" Starkey.

medallion.e: Etymology tree Latin mediālis Early Medieval Latin medālia Italian medagliabor. French médaille French -on French médaillonbor. English medallion Borrowed from French médaillon.

eiffel.e: From French Eiffel, from German Eiffel, Eifel. Family name adopted as a reference to the Eifel mountains.

yamato.e: From Japanese 大和 (Yamato), itself of uncertain derivation, but likely related to 山 (yama, “mountains”). See Proto-Japonic *yamatə.

wilder.e: From wild, probably suggested by wilderness, and as to form by wander.

dyke.e: A variant of dike, from Northern Middle English dik and dike (“ditch”), from Old Norse díki (“ditch”). Influenced by Middle Dutch dijc (“ditch; dam”) and Middle Low German dīk (“dam”). See also ditch.

bailiff.e: From Middle English baillif, baylyf, from Anglo-Norman and Old French bailif (plural bailis), probably from Vulgar Latin *bāiulivus (“castellan”), from Latin bāiulus (“porter; steward”), whence also bail.

peril.e: From Middle English peril, from Old French peril, from Latin perīculum. Doublet of periculum.

holocaust.e: The noun is derived from Middle English holocaust (“burnt offering”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman holocauste, Old French holocauste, olocauste (modern French holocaust), from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient…

io.e: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἰώ (Iṓ, “Io”).

hartley.e: From Old English heorot (“hart, stag”) + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”). Equivalent to hart + -ley (“lea”).

fabio.e: Borrowed from Spanish Fabio, Italian Fabio and Portuguese Fábio.

sleepless.e: From Middle English slepeles, from Old English slǣplēas; equivalent to sleep + -less.

fern.e: From Middle English fern, from Old English fearn, from Proto-West Germanic *farn, from Proto-Germanic *farnaz (“fern”), from Proto-Indo-European *pornóm (“feather, wing; fern, leaf”), from *p(t)erH- (“fern”).

calcium.e: Etymology tree Pre-Greekbor.? Ancient Greek χᾰ́λῐξ (khắlĭx)bor.? substratebor.? Latin calx Proto-Indo-European *-om Proto-Italic *-om Latin -umder.

frown.e: From Middle English frown, froun (“a threatening appearance; lowering of the clouds”), from frounen (“to frown”). See below.

exhaustion.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs Proto-Italic *eks Latin ex Latin ex- Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews-ye-tider.

legislation.e: From Late Latin lēgislātiō (“the giving of the law”). Morphologically legislate + -ion.

discomfort.e: From Middle English discomforten, from Anglo-Norman descomforter, equivalent to dis- + comfort.

technological.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *teḱ- Proto-Indo-European *tetḱ- Proto-Indo-European *téḱ-sneh₂der. Ancient Greek τεχνο- (tekhno-) Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-der.

bermuda.e: Named after Spanish navigator Juan de Bermúdez (1450–c. 1520). See more at Bermúdez.

disperse.e: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

kosher.e: Borrowed from Yiddish כּשר (kosher), from Hebrew כָּשֵׁר (kashér).

entrepreneur.e: Borrowed from French entrepreneur (“one who undertakes or manages”), from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.

siu.e: Borrowed from Cantonese 蕭／萧 (siu1) or 邵 (siu6).

unauthorized.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-West Germanic *un- Old English un- Middle English un- English un- English authorized English unauthorized From un- + authorized.

melbourne.e: Named after William Lamb, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and 2nd Viscount of Melbourne, Derbyshire; ultimately from Old English mylen (“mill”) + burne (“stream”).

flanders.e: From Middle English Flaundres, from Anglo-Norman Flaundre, Flaundres, from Middle Dutch Vlâendren pl, from Vlander, from Old Frisian, from Proto-West Germanic *flaumdr (“waterlogged land”), from *flaum (“flowing, curren…

drinker.e: From Middle English drinkere, drynkere, from Old English drincere (“drinker”), from Proto-Germanic *drinkārijaz (“drinker”), equivalent to drink + -er.

wyoming.e: The state is named after the Wyoming Valley in Pennsylvania, which derives its name from Munsee xwé:wamənk (literally “at the big river flat”). to the Chippewas, the 'oat planters' were known as moonooming.

myrtle.e: From Middle English mirtille, from Old French mirtille, mirtile, from myrte, from Latin myrtillus, from myrtus + -illus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).

cate.e: Aphetized from acate, from Old Northern French acat (“purchase”).

plateau.e: Borrowed from French plateau, diminutive of plat (“a plate”); see plate. Doublet of platter.

sordid.e: Etymology tree Latin sordēs Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁yeti Proto-Italic *-ējō Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁tiinflu.

placement.e: Etymology tree English place Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥tom Proto-Italic *-mentom Latin -mentum Old French -mentbor. Middle English -ment English -ment English placement From place + -ment.

quota.e: From Latin quota pars; see Latin quota.

rockefeller.e: From the German place name Rockenfeld.

bartlett.e: The pear was named by Enoch Bartlett of Dorchester, Massachusetts, after himself.

apparatus.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- Proto-Indo-European *perh₃- Proto-Indo-European *pr̥h₃o- Latin *paro- Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-E…

gringo.e: Borrowed from Spanish gringo, from griego (“Greek”), used for anyone who spoke an unintelligible language. Doublet of Greek.

vancouver.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ep Proto-Indo-European *-o Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó Proto-Indo-European *h₂póder.

samaritan.e: From Latin Samarītānus, from Ancient Greek Σαμαρείτης (Samareítēs), from Σαμαρεία (Samareía, “Samaria”), derived from Biblical Hebrew שֹׁמְרוֹנִים (Šōmərôním) and שֹׁמְרוֹן (Šōmərôn) respectively.

gall.e: From Middle English galle, from Old English ġealla, galla, from Proto-West Germanic *gallā, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.

vend.e: 17th century, likely a backformation from earlier vendible, vendee, vendor inspired by the underlying French vendre, from Old French vendre, from Latin vendere, from vēnum dāre (“to give (something for) sale”).

thelma.e: A literary invention, first appeared in the Swedish novel Kyrkoinvigningen i Hammarby (1840-1841) by Emilie Flygare-Carlén, translated into English as "The Magic Goblet" (1845).

scoring.e: Derivative form of score, initially meaning “groove, notch, cut”, stemming from the same root as shear and scar.

beverage.e: From Middle English beverage, from Old French beverage, variant of bevrage, from beivre (“to drink”), variant of boivre (“to drink”), from Latin bibō. Related to imbibe.

fellowship.e: From Middle English felowschipe, felawshipe, felaȝschyp, equivalent to fellow + -ship; or perhaps adapted from Old Norse félagskapr, félagsskapr (“fellowship”).

tidal.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis Proto-Germanic *tīdiz Proto-West Germanic *tīdi Old English tīd Middle English tyde English t…

genre.e: Unadapted borrowing from French genre, from Old French gen(d)re, borrowed from Latin genere. Doublet of gender and genus.

unfit.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-West Germanic *un- Old English un- Middle English un- English un- Middle English fit? English fit English unfit From un- + fit.

fetus.e: A learned borrowing from Latin fētus (“offspring”). Doublet of fawn.

socialism.e: Attested since 1832; either from French socialisme or from social + -ism.

rosalie.e: From French Rosalie, from the Latin saints’ name Rosālia, from rosa (“rose”). Doublet of Rosalia.

oversight.e: From over- + sight. Verb sense 2 is a semantic loan from German Aufsicht.

reflex.e: From Late Latin reflexus, past participle of reflectere (“to bend back”), equivalent to re- + flex. Photography sense is from noun sense meaning “reflection”. Compare English reflect.

vacate.e: Originally used in the legal sense "to annul", a denominal from Early Modern English vacat (“legal annulment”), a development from Middle English vacat (“absence or cancellation noted in a register”), from Latin vacat,…

goldberg.e: Borrowed from German Goldberg, from German Gold (“gold”) and Berg (“mountain”). One of the ornamental names chosen by Jews who were forced to take surnames in 18th and 19th century Germany.

prosperous.e: From Middle French prospereus, from Old French prosperer, from Latin prosperō (“to cause to succeed”), from Old Latin pro spere (“according to expectation”), from pro (“for”) + spes (“hope”).

inquisition.e: From Old French inquisicion, from Latin inquisitio, from inquirere.

qualification.e: Borrowed from Middle French qualification in the 1540s, which in turn derives from Medieval Latin quālificātiō. By surface analysis, qual(ify) + -ification.

paparazzi.e: From Italian paparazzi, plural of paparazzo.

eater.e: From Middle English eter, etere, etter, from Old English etere; equivalent to eat + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix) (food suitable for eating).

prefect.e: From Middle English prefect and prefecte, from Old French prefect (Mod. French préfet), from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge, overseer, director, prefect”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).

discrimination.e: Learned borrowing from Latin discrīminātiō, discrīminātiōnem, the action noun to discrīminō, discrīmināre (“distinguish”). Equivalent to discriminate + -ion. In English use from the 17th century.

incorporate.e: From Middle English, from Late Latin incorporātus, perfect passive participle of incorporō (“to embody, to incorporate”), from in- (“in”) + corpus, corporis (“body”).

callahan.e: From Irish Ó Ceallacháin, from Ceallachán, diminutive of the given name Ceallach. Doublet of Kelly and Kellogg.

rowdy.e: Possibly from row (“noisy argument”), originally used as a noun.

winslow.e: From Middle English Wynselowe, from Old English Wineshlǣw, from Wines (“Wine's”, personal name) + hlāw (“mound”).

hodges.e: From Hodge, from the given name Roger + patronymic suffix -s.

astronomer.e: From Middle English astronomer, equivalent to astronomy + -er. Displaced native Old English tungolcræftiga.

windsor.e: Inherited from Middle English Wyndelsore, from Old English Windlesōra (“Windsor”, literally “bank with a windlass, winch by the riverside”), from *windel ("reel, winch"; > Middle English windel (“reel, spool”)) + ōra (“…

lobe.e: From Middle French lobe in early 16th century, from New Latin lobus (“a lobe”), from Ancient Greek λοβός (lobós, “the lobe of the ear or of the liver, the pod of a leguminous plant”).

inscription.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Proto-Italic *en Proto-Italic *en- Latin in- Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-?

left-handed.e: From Middle English left handyd, lyfthonded, equivalent to left + handed.

outpost.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úd Proto-Germanic *ūt Proto-Germanic *ūt- Old English ūt- Middle English ut- English out- English post English outpost From out- + post.

snuff.e: Late Middle English, from Middle Dutch snuffen (“to snuff, sniff, snuffle”). Related to Dutch snuiven (“to sniff”), Middle Low German snûve (“pose, head-cold”), German Schnupfen (“head-cold”).

luxurious.e: From Middle English luxurious, from Old French luxurios (modern French luxurieux), from Latin lū̆xuriōsus (“rank, luxuriant, profuse, excessive, immoderate”), from lū̆xuria (“rankness, luxury”), from lū̆xus (“extravagan…

purgatory.e: From Middle English purgatorie, from Old French purgatore, purgatorie, from Latin purgātōrium (“cleansing”). Cognate to English purge.

delilah.e: Borrowed from Hebrew דְּלִילָה (d'līla, “[she who] weakened”).

unimportant.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-West Germanic *un- Old English un- Middle English un- English un- English important English unimportant From un- + important.

moisture.e: From Middle English moisture, from Old French moistour (“moisture, dampness, wetness”). Compare French moiteur.

lefty.e: Etymology tree English left Proto-Germanic *-j-, *-ij- Proto-West Germanic *-i, *-ī Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English lefty From left + -y (nominal suffix).

hendrix.e: A less common spelling of Hendricks, from Hendrick + the patronymic suffix -s.

replica.e: Borrowed from Italian replica, derived from Latin replicare (“to fold or bend back; to reply”). Doublet of reply and replicate.

wondrous.e: From Middle English wondrous, alteration after the suffix -ous of Middle English wonders (“wondrous, wonderful”, adjective), from Old English wundres (“of wonder”), genitive singular of wundor (“wonder, miracle”), from…

horoscope.e: Borrowed from Middle French horoscope, from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”). By surface analysis, horo- + -scope.

hampshire.e: Inherited from Middle English Hampteschire, from Old English Hāmtūnsċīr, from Hāmtūn (“Southampton”) + sċīr (“shire”). For the development of epenthetic /p/, compare Thompson.

morbid.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mer-der.? Latin morbus Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin morbidusder.

optimism.e: From French optimisme, equivalent to Latin optimus + -ism.

humane.e: From Middle English humain, humayne, from Old French humain, umain, from Latin hūmānus, from Latin homō (“man”). Cognate with Old English guma (“man”), whence the groom in English bridegroom.

commodore.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱe? Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Italic *kom Proto-Italic *kom- Latin con- Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂-der.

rink.e: From Middle English rink, renk, from Old English rinc (“man, warrior, hero”), from Proto-Germanic *rankiz (“upright man”), from *rankaz (“straight, upright”), from Proto-Indo-European *reǵ- (“straight, direct”).

initiation.e: Borrowed from Middle French initiation, from Latin initiātiō. Morphologically initiate + -ion.

calamity.e: From Middle French calamité, from Latin calamitās (“loss, damage; disaster”).

nectar.e: From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar, “nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“perish, disappear”) + *-tr̥h₂ (“overcoming”), from *terh₂- (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).

judicial.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂ey- Proto-Indo-European *-u Proto-Indo-European *h₂óyu Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwos Proto-Italic *jowos Latin iūs Proto-Indo-Eur…

swarm.e: From Middle English swarm, from Old English swearm (“swarm, multitude”), from Proto-West Germanic *swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz (“swarm, dizziness”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”).

annabelle.e: A variant of Annabel, by folk etymology, "beautiful Anna".

spartacus.e: Learned borrowing from Latin Spartacus, from Thracian *Spartakos.

trolley.e: Early 19th century (1823) meaning "cart", of dialectal origin (Suffolk), probably from troll (“to trundle, roll”) + -ey (diminutive ending).

theorist.e: Etymology tree Proto-Hellenic *tʰáwā Ancient Greek θέᾱ (théā) Proto-Indo-European *wer-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-der. Proto-Indo-European *weyd-der.

rowan.e: Originally Scots and northern English, from Middle English ron, rone, compare also Northern English raan, ran. At first referring to its fruits, of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse reynir.

density.e: Borrowed from Middle French densité or Latin densitas. Morphologically dense + -ity.

timid.e: Etymology tree Latin timeō Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin timidusder. Middle French timideder.

garth.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos Proto-Germanic *gardaz Old Norse garðrbor.

denton.e: From Old English denu (“valley, den”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

romania.e: From Romanian România, from român (“Romanian”) (in turn from Latin Rōmānus (“Roman”)) + -ia.
s: also used for its former territories

righteousness.e: From earlier rightwiseness, from Middle English rightwisnes, from Old English rihtwīsnes (“justice”), equivalent to righteous + -ness.

confide.e: From Middle Scots confide, confyde (“to put trust in”), from Latin confīdere (“to put trust in, have confidence in”), from con- (“together”) + fidēre (“to trust”).

fencing.e: From Middle English fensing, equivalent to fence + -ing.

laurence.e: From the name of a third century Roman martyr, Latin Laurentius, "a person from Laurentum", the place name possibly derived from laurus (“laurel”).

masturbate.e: A back-formation from masturbation, or else from Latin masturbātus (see -ate), past participle of masturbor. Further derivation of the Latin verb is uncertain; see masturbor for more.

vale.e: From Middle English vale, from Old French val (“valley”), from Latin vallis, valles. Displaced native Old English dell.

wiener.e: Clipping of wienerwurst, from German Wienerwurst (“Vienna sausage”), from Wiener (“of Vienna, Viennese”) + Wurst (“sausage”), because these sausages were originally made in Vienna, Austria.

painless.e: From Middle English paynles, peynlees, equivalent to pain + -less. Compare West Frisian pynleas (“painless”), Dutch pijnloos (“painless”).

eruption.e: From Middle French éruption, from Latin eruptio.

mojo.e: Probably of Creole origin, cognate with Gullah moco (“witchcraft”), Fula moco'o (“medicine man”). The origin of the drug sense is uncertain, possibly related to Spanish mojar (“to toast (celebrate with a drink)”).

essex.e: Inherited from Old English Ēastseaxan (literally “East Saxons”), which stood for both Essex and the people of Essex.

eternally.e: From Middle English eternally, eternaly; equivalent to eternal + -ly.

repulsive.e: Borrowed from Middle French repulsif, from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus. By surface analysis, repuls(e) + -ive.

ness.e: Named after the River Ness, of Proto-Brythonic/Pictish origin, from a Proto-Celtic word *Nesta describing great currents, according to MacBain, from the same Proto-Indo-European root that gave the river Νέστος (Néstos),…

devise.e: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.

impeccable.e: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).

crucify.e: From Middle English crucifien, from Old French crucefier, from Late Latin crucificō, from Latin crucifigō.

customary.e: From Middle English custumary, from Medieval Latin custumarius. By surface analysis, custom + -ary.

costly.e: From Middle English costly, costely, costeley, equivalent to cost + -ly.

simplicity.e: From Middle English simplicite, from Old French simplicite, from Latin simplicitās, from simplex (“simple”). See simple. By surface analysis, simple + -icity. Partially displaced native English onefoldness.

carr.e: From Middle English kerr and Middle English carr meaning meadow, field or grassland of a low lying variety; possibly related to Old Norse kjarr. Compare Swedish kärr, Icelandic kjarr.

nichols.e: From Nichol, medieval vernacular form of the given name Nicholas + the patronymic suffix -s.

setback.e: Deverbal from set back. Compare drawback.

clockwork.e: Etymology tree Proto-Celtic *klokkosder. Early Medieval Latin cloccader. Old Northern French cloquebor. Old Dutch *klokka Middle Dutch clockebor.

brawl.e: The verb is derived from Late Middle English braulen, brall, brallen (“to clamour, to shout; to quarrel; to boast”); further etymology is uncertain, but the word could be related to bray and ultimately imitative.

bog.e: Inherited from Middle English bog (originally chiefly in Ireland and Scotland), from Irish and Scottish Gaelic bogach (“soft, boggy ground”), from Old Irish bog (“soft”), from Proto-Celtic *buggos (“soft, tender”) + Old…

tex.e: The letters of the name are meant to represent the capital Greek letters Τ (tau), Ε (epsilon), and Χ (chi), as TeX is an abbreviation of Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē), which is also the root word of technical.

gob.e: From Middle English gobbe (also Middle English gobet), from Old French gobet, gobe (“lump, mouthful”), from Transalpine Gaulish *gobbo- (“neb, muzzle”).

lancaster.e: From Middle English Lancaster, Loncastre, the name of the Roman fort on the River Lune, from Lune + the Old English suffix ceaster (“town”), found in many placenames.

godfrey.e: From Old French Godefrei, from Old High German Godafrid (“peace of God”), from Proto-Germanic *Gudafriþuz. Equivalent to god + frith. Doublet of Gottfried and Geoffrey.

novelty.e: From Middle English novelte, from Old French novelté (Modern French nouveauté), from the adjective novel, ultimately from Latin novellus. By surface analysis, novel + -ty.

doubtful.e: From Middle English doutfull, douteful, equivalent to doubt + -ful.

reproduce.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *per-der.? Proto-Indo-European *per-der.?

blueberry.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- Proto-Indo-European *-eh₁- Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁-der. Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁wos Proto-Germanic *blēwaz Proto-West Germanic *blāubor.

ryu.e: From Japanese 流(りゅう) (ryū), mainly an affix, used here in the sense of 流派(りゅうは) (ryūha).

algeria.e: Etymology tree Arabic جَزَائِر بَنِي مَزْغَنَّى (jazāʔir banī mazḡannā)ellip. Arabic الْجَزَائِر (al-jazāʔir)bor. French Algerbor.

geometry.e: Etymology tree Pre-Greek der. Proto-Hellenic *gayader. Ancient Greek γαῖᾰ (gaîă)clip.

bahamas.e: Disputed; probably from Spanish baja mar (“shallow sea”) or Taíno ba ha ma (“big upper middle land”), via Spanish.

horizontal.e: Borrowed from Middle French horizontal, from horizon, horizonte, from Latin horizōn (stem horizont-).

fertilizer.e: Etymology tree English fertilize Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

hinge.e: From Middle English henge (“hinge”), from Old English *henġ or *henġe (“hinge”), from Proto-West Germanic *hangiju or *hangī; compare Old English *henġe- in henġeclif (“overhanging cliff”), Old English henġen (“hanging;…

zhu.e: The atonal Hanyu Pinyin romanization of Mandarin 銖 /铢 (zhū).

helium.e: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the Sun's atmosphere) with the suffix + -ium. Probably coined by Norman Lockyer.
s: E939 when used as a packaging gas

restriction.e: From Middle English restriccioun, from Anglo-Norman restriction, Middle French restriction, and their source, Late Latin restrictiō, from Latin restringō. Morphologically restrict + -ion.

trait.e: Borrowed from Middle French trait (“line, feature”), from Latin tractus (“drawing, pulling”), from Latin trahō. Doublet of tract.

implement.e: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).

supervise.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin supervisus, from supervidere, from Latin super + videre. Doublet of survey.

evident.e: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns,…

skank.e: Unknown. Perhaps from skag (“unattractive woman”), but the origins of skag are unknown. Compare scold (“troublesome woman”), skeevy (“disgusting”). Attested from the 1960s.

drool.e: From earlier drule, apparently a corruption of drivel (compare snool from snivel). Compare also Middle English drullen (“to stagger, drool”), Dutch druilen (“to be listless, snooze”).

coastal.e: Etymology tree Latin costa Latin costicāreder. Old French costoierbor. Middle English costeien English coast Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.?

matrimony.e: From Old French matremoine, from Latin mātrimōnium (“marriage, wedlock”), from mātri(s) (“mother”) + -mōnium (“obligation”). By surface analysis, matri- + -mony. Compare patrimony.

sensual.e: From Late Latin sensualis (“endowed with feeling, sensual”), from Latin sensus (“feeling, sense”).

lennon.e: From Irish Ó Leannáin (“descendant of Lover (Leannán)”) and from Ó Lonáin (“descendant of Blackbird (Lonán)”).

hutton.e: From Old English hōh (“ridge, spur”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”).

rugged.e: From Middle English rugged, roggyd, ruggyd, derived from Old Norse rǫgg (“tuft, shagginess”), equivalent to rug (“rough, woollen material”) + -ed.

potassium.e: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1807, from potassa (a Latinized form of potash) + -ium.

childbirth.e: From Middle English childbyrth [and other forms], perhaps a partial calque of Old Norse barnburðr (“childbearing, childbirth”, literally “bairn birth”); equivalent to child + birth.

livelihood.e: From Middle English liflode, from Old English līflād (“course of life, conduct”), from līf (“life”) + lād (“course, journey”), later altered under the influence of lively, -hood. Compare life, lode.

catfish.e: From cat + fish. Likely so named for its prominent barbels like a cat's whiskers. Compare West Frisian katfisk (“catfish”), Dutch katvis (“catfish”). Compare also German Seekatze (“catfish”, literally “sea-cat”).

charger.e: From Middle English chargere, equivalent to charge + -er.

outing.e: From out + -ing. Compare Old English yting ("outing, journey").

una.e: Anglicized form of Irish Úna. Doublet of Oona.

glitch.e: Probably borrowed from Yiddish גליטש (glitsh), from German glitschig (“slippy”), from glitschen (“to slide, glide, slip”) + -ig (“-y”). Related to gleiten (“glide”). Cognate with French glisser (“to slip, slide, skid”).

jell-o.e: Trademarked by Pearle Bixby Wait and named by his wife, May Wait.

grants.e: From Grant + -s. , John R. and Lewis A. Grant, who were awarded a contract to build a section of the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad through the region.

criteria.e: The plural form of criterion, formed according to the Ancient Greek -ον (-on) → -α (-a) pluralisation pattern.

poe.e: A nickname from Old Norse pái (“peacock”). This surname is also well established in Ireland.

samba.e: Borrowed from Brazilian Portuguese samba, from a Bantu language. Doublet of semba.

silicon.e: Coined by Scottish chemist Thomas Thomson as a modification of the earlier name silicium, from the stem of Latin silex (“flint, silica”) + -on from carbon.

rohan.e: Habitational surname from Rohan in Morbihan, Brittany. Also a variant of Rowan and Ruane.

dyson.e: A patronymic English surname, from Dennis + -son, compare Tyson, Tennyson.

invaluable.e: From in- + valuable (compare priceless). Piecewise doublet of unvaluable.

crossword.e: From cross + word. Various word puzzles referred to as "crosswords" date back to the 1860s.

undead.e: From Middle English undede, equivalent to un- + dead. The first attestation is from around 1400.

roster.e: Borrowed from Dutch rooster (“gridiron, table, list”), from Middle Dutch roosten (“to roast”). More at roast.

grinder.e: From Middle English grinder, grindere, from Old English grindere (“one or that which grinds; grinder”), equivalent to grind + -er.

weber.e: Named after the German physicist Wilhelm Eduard Weber

kincaid.e: Scottish habitational surname from a minor place near Lennoxtown, from Scottish Gaelic ceann (“head, top”) + càithe (“pass”) or cadha (“quagmire”).

mendoza.e: Borrowed from Spanish Mendoza, from Basque Mendoza.

tracing.e: From Middle English tracyng; equivalent to trace + -ing.

wham.e: Onomatopoeic, representing the sound of an object being slammed against something.

nemo.e: From Latin nemo. The "clownfish" meaning comes from the film Finding Nemo, where Nemo is a clownfish.

docking.e: From Middle English dockyng. By surface analysis, dock + -ing.

cowardice.e: From Middle English cowardise, borrowed from Anglo-Norman cuardise (modern French couardise).

instagram.e: Trade name. Blend of instant + telegram. By surface analysis, insta- + -gram.

curt.e: From the Latin curtus (“shortened”). Cognate with Dutch kort, German kurz, Galician curto, French court, Italian corto, Portuguese curto, and Spanish corto. Doublet of short.

stamina.e: From Latin stāmina, plural of stāmen.

cheesecake.e: From Middle English chesekake; equivalent to cheese + cake. Compare chess cake.

lise.e: From the French, and possible also from Scandinavian, Lise. Variant of more common English Lisa.

upbringing.e: From Middle English upbringinge, equivalent to upbring + -ing.

geronimo.e: Various theories; see Wikipedia. In any case, likely ultimately from the name of Geronimo the Apache. Originally used by American paratroopers.

welles.e: Named after Well, Lincolnshire, from Old English wielle (“fountain, spring”). Cognate with English well.

streaming.e: From Middle English stremyng, stremynge, stremande, equivalent to stream + -ing.

navigator.e: From Latin nāvigātor. By surface analysis, navigate + -or.

cleaver.e: From Middle English clevere, equivalent to cleave + -er.

anew.e: From Middle English onew, of newe, from Old English of niowe. By surface analysis, a- (“of, from”) + new.

spam.e: The original sense (canned ham) is a proprietary name registered by Geo. A. Hormel & Co. , 1937.

teeny.e: Alteration of tiny, possibly with a childish or fanciful intention. First attested in 1825.

romano.e: Borrowed from Italian romano (“Roman”). Doublet of Roman.

hyderabad.e: Borrowed from Hindi हैदराबाद (haidarābād) / Urdu حَیْدَر آبَاد (haydar ābād), from हैदर (haidar) / حَیْدَر (haydar, “lion”) + -आबाद (-ābād) / آبَاد (ābād, placename suffix).

chino.e: A term used by American veterans of the Spanish-American war. It is theorized that the cloth or the trousers were made in China.

recreation.e: From Middle English recreacion, from Middle French recreacion, from Old French recreacion, from Latin recreātiō.

fatima.e: From Arabic فَاطِمَة (fāṭima). The name Fatima is from the Arabic root f-t-m (lit. 'to wean') and signifies the Shia belief that she, her progeny, and her adherents (Shi'a) have been spared from hellfire.

molest.e: From Middle English molesten, from Old French molester, from Latin molestō (“to trouble, annoy, molest”), from molestus (“troublesome”), from moles (“a burden, difficulty, labor, trouble”); see mole.

believable.e: From Middle English bilevable, beleevable, equivalent to believe + -able.

widower.e: From Middle English widwere, equivalent to widow + -er.

versailles.e: Borrowed from French Versailles, of uncertain Latin origin (see French entry below), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn around”).
s: dictate of Versailles / Dictate of Versailles

draper.e: From Middle English draper, from Anglo-Norman draper, from Old French drapier, from drap + -ier.

sook.e: Probably from suck. Compare sukey (attested 1838), Sucky (1844), Suke (1850); sook from 1906.

exploitation.e: Borrowed from French exploitation, from exploiter (“exploit”), from Latin explicō (“unfold, deploy”). By surface analysis, exploit + -ation.

summary.e: From Middle English summary, from Medieval Latin summārius, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives).

joanie.e: From Joan + -ie. Doublet of Ivanka, Jan, Janelle, Janet, Janey, Janine, Jeanette, Jeanie, Jeannette, Jeannine, Jen, Jenna, Jenny, Jessy, Jo, Jody, Juanita, Shanae, Sinead, and Vanna.

informal.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English in- English formal English informal From in- + formal.
s: not in accord with the usual regulations

promptly.e: Etymology tree English prompt Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder.

dover.e: From Old English Dofras, from Latin Dubris, from Brythonic Dubras (“the waters”), from Proto-Celtic *dubros (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰubrós (“dark”), from *dʰewb- (“deep”). Compare Tauber.

faithfully.e: From Middle English feithfulli, equivalent to faithful + -ly.

gemini.e: BA, “the Divine Twins, in Mesopotamia identified as Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea; name of constellation”). See Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea.

leech.e: From Middle English leche (“blood-sucking worm”), from Old English lǣċe (“blood-sucking worm”), akin to Middle Dutch lāke ("blood-sucking worm"; > modern Dutch laak).

sassy.e: A modification of saucy, equivalent to sass + -y, originally used in American English. First attested in 1799, but in common usage only as of the mid-19th century.

vegetation.e: Borrowed from Middle French végétation, from Medieval Latin vegetātiōnem.

nab.e: From dialectal nap (“to seize, lay hold of”), probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Swedish nappa (“to pluck, pinch”).

lim.e: From Korean, including 임 (Im), 林 or 任; 림 (Rim), 林.

carton.e: Borrowed from French carton, from Italian cartone. Doublet of cartoon.

scapegoat.e: From scape + goat; coined by English biblical scholar and translator William Tyndale, interpreting Biblical Hebrew עֲזָאזֵל (“azazél”) (Leviticus 16:8, 10, 26), from an interpretation as coming from עֵז (ez, “goat”) and…

burr.e: From Middle English burre, perhaps related to Old English byrst (“bristle”). Cognate with Danish burre, borre (“burdock, burr”), Swedish borre (“sea-urchin”).

north dakota.e: The state was formed from northern portion of the former Dakota Territory.

regroup.e: Borrowed from French regrouper. By surface analysis, re- + group.

heller.e: Borrowed from German Heller. Doublet of halier.

machete.e: From Spanish machete, diminutive of macho (“sledgehammer”), from Latin mattea, possibly from mactare (“slaughter in sacrifice”); cognate with Old French machier, French massue, English mace.

rebellious.e: From Middle English rebellious; equivalent to rebel + -ious.

reconcile.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re- Proto-Indo-European *ḱe?

eunuch.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek εὐνή (eunḗ) Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ-der.

captivity.e: From Middle English captivite, from Latin captīvitās. By surface analysis, captive + -ity. Entered into the English lexicon around the 14th century.

aroma.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma)bor. Late Latin arōmatader. English aroma From Late Latin arōmata (“spices”) (or arōma (“spice”)), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).

manila.e: From Spanish Manila, from Tagalog Maynila, from may (“there is”) + nila (“indigo”), Tagalog nila from Sanskrit नील (nīla).

snowball.e: From Middle English snoweball, snoweballe, snaweballe, snayballe, equivalent to snow + ball.

atlas.e: Borrowed from Latin Atlas, from the name of the Ancient Greek mythological figure Ἄτλας (Átlas, “Bearer (of the Heavens)”), from τλῆναι (tlênai, “to suffer”, “to endure”, “to bear”).

volt.e: Named after Italian physicist Alessandro Volta. For the surname, see Italian Volta.

yolanda.e: From Spanish Yolanda, the form of a medieval royal name of obscure, probably Germanic, origin. It has been identified with Latin Violante and with Ancient Greek ἴον (íon, “violet”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

evasive.e: From French évasif, from Latin ēvādō.

watkins.e: From a medieval diminutive of the given name Walter + the patronymic suffix -s.

bimbo.e: From Italian bimbo (“a child, a male baby”), variant of bambino (“child”).

starbucks.e: Etymology tree Old Norse stor Old Norse bekkr English Starbeck English Starbuck English -'s English -s English Starbucks From Starbuck (surname) + -s.

dada.e: Imitative of a child's first syllables; see dad.

ballad.e: From French ballade, from Old Occitan ballada (“poem for a dance”), from Late Latin ballare. Doublet of balada and ballade.

haystack.e: From Middle English haystak, haystake, hey stak, equivalent to hay + stack.

penniless.e: From Middle English penyles, penylees; equivalent to penny + -less. Compare Old Norse penningalauss (“penniless”).

wrongly.e: From Middle English wrongly, wrongliche, equivalent to wrong + -ly.

sandoval.e: From Spanish, named after the city in Burgos Province, Spain, from Old Spanish Sannoval, from Latin saltus (“grove”) + novālis (“newly cleared land”).

sweeney.e: Anglicized form of Irish Ó Suibhne. Compare McSweeney.

patiently.e: Etymology tree English patient Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder.

birch.e: PIE word *bʰerHǵós From Middle English birche, birk, from Old English birċe, bierċe, from Proto-West Germanic *birkijā, from Proto-Germanic *birkijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵos.

incompetence.e: From French incompétence, equivalent to in- + competence.

spartan.e: By analogy with the ancient Spartans, who famously possessed these qualities.

prohibition.e: From Anglo-Norman and Old French prohibicion, from Latin prohibitiō. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ion.

oakland.e: By proprialization of oak + -land, as likewise with Oakwood from oakwood.

skateboard.e: From skate + board. The foot-treadable skateboard sense (noun sense 1) came first (mid-20th century). The vehicle chassis sense (noun sense 2) was named for its resemblance thereto (late 20th or early 21st century).

lew.e: From corruption of French louis, from Louis, presumably Louis IX or Louis XI, who issued gold écus.

aviation.e: Borrowed from French aviation, derived from Latin avis (“bird”). By surface analysis, avi- + -ation.

wilhelm.e: Borrowed from German Wilhelm. Doublet of William.

inferno.e: From Italian inferno (“hell”), from Latin infernus (“of the lower regions”), inferna (“the lower regions”); see infernal. The meaning "big fire" came as a figurative use from the traditional idea of hellfire.

swoop.e: Etymology tree Proto-Germanic *swaipaną Proto-West Germanic *swaipan Old English swāpan Middle English swopen English swoop Inherited from Middle English swopen (“to sweep”), from Old English swāpan. Doublet of swaip.

raines.e: From Anglo-Norman Reins, Middle French Reins, variant of Reims, the French town where the fabric was originally produced.

whorehouse.e: From Middle English horehous, equivalent to whore + house.

megatron.e: Blend of Meghan + -tron (influenced in form by Megatron, a fictional character among the Transformers, whose name was influenced by megatron, mega-, M, and -tron).

mambo.e: From Haitian Creole manbo (“voodoo priestess”) (ultimately from Yoruba mambo (“to talk”)), in later senses via Cuban Spanish mambo (“dance”).

shoplifting.e: By surface analysis, shoplift + -ing. The noun sense (from 1690) predates the verb.

jukebox.e: First use appears c. 1939, from juke (“roadside café”) + box, replacing older collocational terms such as nickel-in-a-slot phonograph, coin-in-the-slot phonograph, and coin-operated phonograph.

krista.e: A spelling variant of Christa, a modern short form of Christina, partly borrowed from German Christa.

haiti.e: From Taíno hayiti (“land of lofty barrows or mountains”), which was the native name given to the whole island of Hispaniola.

mouthful.e: From Middle English mouthful, mouth-full, mouthe full, from Old English *mūþfull, from Proto-West Germanic *munþafull, equivalent to mouth + -ful.

algebra.e: Etymology tree Arabic جَبَرَ (jabara) Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr)bor. Medieval Latin algebrabor.

luka.e: From the common Slavic (Macedonian, Russian, Serbo-Croatian, and Ukrainian, etc) male given name Luka and from Macedonian, Russian, and Ukrainian Лука́ (Luká), all cognates of English Luke and Lucas.

conor.e: From Irish Conchúr, from Old Irish Conchobar (“lover of hounds”).

pandora.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- Proto-Indo-European *-énts Proto-Indo-European *ph₂énts? Proto-Hellenic *pánts Ancient Greek πᾶς (pâs)der.

disadvantage.e: From Middle English disavauntage, from Old French desavantage.

headless.e: From Middle English heedles, hevedles, from Old English hēafodlēas (“headless”), equivalent to head + -less.

ganga.e: From French ganga, from Catalan ganga.

berserk.e: The noun is borrowed from Old Norse berserkr (“Norse warrior who fights in a frenzy”), probably from bjǫrn (“bear”) + serkr (“coat; shirt”), referring to the bearskins which the warriors wore.

flack.e: From Middle English flacken (“to palpitate, flutter”), from Old English *flaccian, from Proto-West Germanic *flakkōn, from Proto-Germanic *flakkōną (“to beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ-, which could be related to…

adamant.e: From Middle English adamant, adamaunt, from Latin adamantem, accusative singular form of adamās (“hard as steel”), from Ancient Greek ἀδάμαντ- (adámant-, “invincible”), oblique stem of ἀδάμας (adámas).

distinctly.e: Etymology tree English distinct Middle English -ly English -ly English distinctly From distinct + -ly.

rupture.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *Hrew-? Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- Proto-Indo-European *-né- Proto-Indo-European *Hrunépti Latin rumpō Latin ruptūrader. Middle French rupturebor. ▲ Latin ruptūrabor.

arlene.e: A nineteenth-century coinage probably based on similar-sounding names such as Charlene and Arlette.

celery.e: From French céleri, from Lombard selleri, a plural of Latin selīnum, from Ancient Greek σέλῑνον (sélīnon). Displaced English march (“celery, smallage”) and smallage (“wild celery”).

conveniently.e: Etymology tree English convenient Middle English -ly English -ly English conveniently From convenient + -ly.

foil.e: Acronym of first outer inner last or similar.

jaffa.e: Etymology tree Biblical Hebrew יָפוֹ (yāfō)bor. Arabic يَافَا (yāfā)bor. English Jaffa Borrowed from Arabic يَافَا (yāfā), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew יָפוֹ (yāfō).

man-made.e: From man (“human”) + made. First attested in 1615. According to the OED, the pronunciation with primary stress on man, /ˈmænˌmeɪd/, is older.

slum.e: First attested in 1812. Originally slang, in the sense "room", especially "backroom", of unknown origin.

landry.e: French, from the Germanic land, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), + ric, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“mighty”). Cognate to the Spanish given name Landerico, Landrigo.

palestinian.e: Etymology tree English Palestine Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Italic *-nos Proto-Italic *-ānos Latin -ānus Latin -iānusbor.

hap.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kob-der. Proto-Germanic *hampą Old Norse happbor.

maw.e: From Middle English mawe, maghe, maȝe, from Old English maga (“stomach; maw”), from Proto-West Germanic *magō, from Proto-Germanic *magô (“belly; stomach”), from Proto-Indo-European *mak-, *maks- (“bag, bellows, belly”).

rapper.e: Etymology tree English rap Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

vogue.e: First attested in 1565. Borrowed from Middle French vogue (“wave, course of success”), from Old French vogue, from voguer (“to row, sway, set sail”), from Old Saxon wogōn (“to sway, rock”), var.

daisuke.e: Borrowed from Japanese だいすけ (Daisuke).

eureka.e: From Ancient Greek εὕρηκα (heúrēka, “I have found”), perfect active indicative first person singular of εὑρίσκω (heurískō, “to find”).

privy.e: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”). Doublet of private.

encryption.e: Etymology tree English encrypt Proto-Indo-European *-tis Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō Proto-Italic *-tiō Latin -tiō Latin -ātiōlbor. Old French -ationbor.

burrow.e: From Middle English borowe, borewe, borwȝ, burȝe, burh, burye (“refuge for an animal, lair, burrow”), apparently a variant of Middle English burgh (“fortified dwelling, stronghold, refuge”) (see borough) and thus from O…

hoist.e: Alteration of earlier hoise (“to hoist”), apparently based on the past tense forms, from Middle Dutch hisen (“to hoist”). Compare modern Dutch hijsen (“to hoist”), German hissen (“to hoist”), Danish hejse (“to hoist”).

emphasis.e: From Latin emphasis, from Ancient Greek ἔμφασις (émphasis, “significance”), from ἐμφαίνω (emphaínō, “to present; to indicate”), from ἐν- (en-, “in”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to show”).

moderate.e: From Middle English moderat(e) (“moderate, temperate”), borrowed from Latin moderātus, perfect active participle of moderor (“to regulate, to restrain, to moderate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from moder-, m…

retro.e: Borrowed from French rétro, ultimately from Latin retro.

cincinnati.e: Named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which is named after Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus; see Latin Cincinnāti and Cincinnātus.

sociopath.e: From socio- + -path. First use appears c. 1914.

elmo.e: From an Italian contraction of Erasmo, cognate with Erasmus. Also a German short form of Elmar. * By folk etymology seen as a short form of Elmer.

nighttime.e: From Middle English nyght tyme, nyȝttyme, equivalent to night + time. Compare Dutch nachttijd, German Nachtzeit, Danish nattetid, Swedish nattetid.

namely.e: From Middle English namely, nameliche, namelike, equivalent to name + -ly.

delaney.e: From a Norman baronial surname, from a place in France, Old French del aunaie (“from the alder grove”). In Ireland an anglicization of Irish Ó Dubhshláine (descendant of Black (dubh) + Challenge (slán)).

cannabis.e: Learned borrowing from Latin cannabis (“hemp”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). See there for more. Further reading at Etymology of cannabis on Wikipedia. Doublet of canvas and hemp.

uncanny.e: From un- + canny; thus “beyond one's ken,” or outside one's familiar knowledge or perceptions. Compare Middle English unkanne (“unknown”).

salaam.e: From Arabic سَلَام (salām, “peace”). Doublet of shalom, a borrowing from Hebrew.

rainforest.e: From rain + forest, a calque of German Regenwald.

ebay.e: Short for Echo Bay Technology Group, the consulting firm involved with its development. By surface analysis, e- (digital) + bay.

kelvin.e: Named after Irish-born Scottish physicist William Thomson, Lord Kelvin.

ridicule.e: The obsolete adjective is borrowed from French ridicule, from Latin rīdiculus (“laughable, comical, amusing, absurd, ridiculous”), from ridere (“to laugh”).

yue.e: The atonal pinyin romanization of the standard Mandarin pronunciation of Chinese 龠 (yuè).

chronicle.e: From Middle English cronicle, cronycle, from Anglo-Norman cronicle, from Old French cronike, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós, “of or concerning time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”).

trample.e: From Middle English tramplen, trampelen (“to walk heavily”), equivalent to tramp + -le.

mules.e: From the surname of the procedure's inventor, John Mules.

piglet.e: From pig + -let (diminutive suffix). Attested from 1855. Displaced Old English fearh.

band-aid.e: Genericized trademark from Band-Aid, registered and coined by Johnson & Johnson in 1924 as band(age) + aid.

alba.e: First attested in 1821; borrowed from Occitan alba, ultimately from Latin albus (“white”); compare Spanish alba (“dawn”).

persuasion.e: From French persuasion and its source, Latin persuāsiō, from persuādēre, from suādēre (“to advise, recommend”).

tuesdays.e: Etymology tree English Tuesday Middle English -es English -s English Tuesdays From Tuesday + -s (adverb suffix).

inability.e: From earlier inhability (“disqualification for office”), equivalent to in- + ability. Compare Middle French inhabilité, Medieval Latin inhabilitās.

quincy.e: A Norman surname of Old French origin, from a place name Quincy or Quincey in France, ultimately from Latin Quintus (“fifth [born]”).

shalom.e: Borrowed from Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (šālóm, “peace, well-being; Hello, good-bye”). Doublet of salaam, the same word via Arabic.

hes.e: A mixture of she and he. Coined by Ching Hai in 1990s.

orthodox.e: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).

bosnia.e: From the name of the river Bosna.

wuss.e: 1976–1981 in US college slang. Perhaps abbreviated from wussy, or blend of wimp and puss. Compare earlier wussy.

detonation.e: From French détonation; equivalent to detonate + -ion.

cylon.e: Learned borrowing from Latin Cylōn or its etymon Ancient Greek Κῠ́λων (Kŭ́lōn).

evict.e: From Middle English evicten, evycten, borrowed from Latin ēvictus, past participle of ēvincō (“to vanquish completely”). Doublet of evince.

mailed.e: From Middle English mayled; equivalent to mail (“chainmail; spot on a bird's feather”) + -ed.

untrue.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-Indo-European *drewH-der.

bland.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *mel- Proto-Indo-European *meld- Proto-Indo-European *mland-der. Latin blandusbor. English bland Borrowed from Latin blandus (“pleasant”).

ancestral.e: From Anglo-Norman ancestrel, from ancestre (“ancestor”), equivalent to ancestor + -al.

flattery.e: From Middle English flaterye, flaterie, from Old French flaterie, from the verb flater (“to flatter”). By surface analysis, flatter + -y (forming abstract nouns).

unspeakable.e: From Middle English unspekable, equivalent to un- + speakable.

reincarnation.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor.

marin.e: The county was either named after Chief Marin, of the Coast Miwok tribe, or derived from the Spanish name of its eastern bay known as Bahía de Nuestra Señora del Rosario la Marinera in 1775.

muster.e: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”).

schizophrenic.e: Etymology tree English schizophrenia Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English schizophrenic From schizophrenia + -ic.

bangalore.e: From Kannada ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು (beṅgaḷūru). See Bengaluru for details.

painfully.e: From Middle English peinfully, paynefully, equivalent to painful + -ly.

mindless.e: From Middle English myndles, myndelees, myndeles, mendlees, from Old English myndlēas, ġemyndlēas (“foolish, senseless”), equivalent to mind + -less.

unheard.e: From Middle English unherd, unherde, from Old English unġehīered (“unheard”), equivalent to un- + heard. Cognate with West Frisian ûnheard (“unheard”), Dutch ongehoord (“unheard”), German ungehört (“unheard”).

cisco.e: From French ciscoette (“siscowet”), from Ojibwe siscowet (“cooks itself”).

flashy.e: Etymology tree English flash Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English flashy From flash + -y.

commend.e: From Middle English commenden, from Old French comender, from Latin commendō (“commend, entrust to, commit, recommend”), from com- + mandō (“to commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand”) + dō (“to put”).

cinch.e: Borrowed from Occitan cencha, from Latin cincta, or from Spanish cincha (“a belt or girth”), from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum. Doublet of cingle.

mater.e: From Latin māter (“mother”), partly via Late Middle English matere. Doublet of mata and mother. Ancestor of matrix.

gen.e: Shortened from new generation, from Italian generazione nuova.

participant.e: From stem of particip(ate) + -ant, borrowed from Middle French participant, from Latin participāns, present participle of participō; see participate. Displaced native Old English dǣlnimend (literally “part taker”).

conan.e: From Irish Conán, from Middle Irish Conán, from Primitive Irish ᚉᚑᚅᚐᚅᚅ (conann), a derivative of Proto-Celtic *kū (“dog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.

mackerel.e: From Middle English mackerell, macrell, macrelle, makarell, makerel, makerell, makerelle, makrel, makrell, makyrelle, from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown.

loki.e: Borrowed from Old Norse Loki, where further etymology is shown.

thereby.e: From Middle English therby, from Old English ðǣrbig, equivalent to there + by. Compare the parallel formation of German dabei.

reilly.e: From Irish Ó Raghallaigh, a surname meaning "descendants of Raghallach".

lagoon.e: Borrowed from French lagune, from Italian laguna, from Latin lacūna. Related to Old English lagu via Proto-Indo-European. Doublet of lacuna and lacune.

merciless.e: From Middle English merciles, mercyles, equivalent to mercy + -less.

bouncer.e: Etymology tree English bounce Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

speck.e: From Middle English spekke, from Old English specca (“small spot, stain”), from the same ultimate source as Proto-Germanic *sprakô (“spark”). Cognate with Low German spaken (“to spot with wet”).

lifeless.e: From Middle English lyfles, lifles, from Old English līflēas (“lifeless”), equivalent to life + -less.

westminster.e: From the abbey of Westminster; from Middle English Westmynster, from Old English Westmynster; equivalent to west + minster.

donner.e: From Afrikaans donder (“thrash”), from Dutch donder (“thunder”). Doublet of thunder.

lancelot.e: From Middle English Launcelot, from Old French Lancelot, from Frankish *Lanzo, hypocoristic form of names beginning in *Land-, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), and diminutive Old French endings -el and -ot.

amish.e: From Pennsylvania German Amisch or German Amische, after the name of the Swiss preacher Jakob Amman (1645-1730). The surname is a contraction of Old High German ambahtman.

ophelia.e: Borrowed from Italian Ofelia, coined by the poet Jacopo Sannazaro in his poem Arcadia (1504), probably from the Ancient Greek ὠφέλειᾰ (ōphéleiă, “help, aid, succour”).

mart.e: From Middle Dutch mart, markt (“market”) (Modern Dutch markt), from Old Dutch *markat, from Late Latin marcātus, an alternative form of Classical Latin mercātus. See market.

sympathize.e: Borrowed from French sympathiser. By surface analysis, sympathy + -ize. Displaced native Old English efnþrōwian (literally “to suffer with or together”).

susanna.e: From Ancient Greek Σουσάννα (Sousánna), the New Testament form of Hebrew שׁוֹשַׁנָּה (šōšannā, “lily”).

fad.e: Of English dialectal origin. Further origin obscure.

dwelling.e: From Middle English dwellynge, dwellyng (“delay, continuance, abode”), equivalent to dwell + -ing. More at dwell.

singular.e: From Middle English singuler, from Old French, from Latin singulāris (“alone of its kind”), from Latin singulus (“single”).

loathe.e: From Middle English lothe, from Old English lāþian, from Proto-West Germanic *laiþēn, from Proto-Germanic *laiþāną. Cognate with Old Norse leiðask ( > Danish ledes, Icelandic leiðast, all reflexive), German Leid.

lurch.e: Originally a nautical term, found in lee-larches (“the sudden and violent rolls of a ship to the leeward in high seas”), of unknown origin.

ultimatum.e: From Latin ultimatus (“late, last final”), from Latin ultimus (“extreme, last, furthest, farthest, final”).

pedophile.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w-der. Proto-Hellenic *pā́wits Ancient Greek παιδ- (paid-)lbor.

directive.e: From Middle French directif. The noun senses are from French directive (feminine form of the adjective).

thermometer.e: Borrowed from French thermomètre; equivalent to thermo- + -meter.

persona.e: Borrowed from Latin persōna (“mask; character”), of uncertain origin.

pritchard.e: Anglicised from Welsh patronymic prefix ap + Richard.

arkansas.e: From the name of the Arkansas River, from French Arcansas, a (plural) designation of either a Siouan tribe or the Quapaw.

norfolk.e: From Middle English Northfolk, from Old English Norþfolc (literally “northern people”), from norþ (“north, northern”) + folc (“folk, people, race, nation”), equivalent to north + folk.

yamamoto.e: Borrowed from Japanese 山本 (Yamamoto), meaning "(one who lives at) the base of the mountain(s)" or "(one from) Yamamoto District".

askin.e: * As an English surname of Norman origin, from a shortened form of the name Asketin, a diminutive of Old Norse Ásketill, from Áskell, see also Haskell. * Also as an English surname, from Askern in Campsall.

haze.e: * The earliest instances are of the latter part of the 17th century. * Possibly back-formation from hazy. * Compare Old Norse höss (“grey”), akin to Old English hasu (“gray”).

macau.e: Borrowed from Portuguese Macau, from Hokkien. See Portuguese Macau for more info.

bazaar.e: From Middle French bazar or Italian bazar, from Ottoman Turkish بازار (bazar), from Persian بازار (bâzâr).

walnut.e: From Middle English walnote, walnutte, walnotte, from Old English wealhhnutu (“walnut”, literally “foreign nut”), from Proto-Germanic *walhahnuts (literally “foreigner-nut”).

swallowing.e: Inherited from Middle English swolwynge; by surface analysis, swallow + -ing.

plutonium.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploûtos) Proto-Indo-European *-Hō Ancient Greek -ων (-ōn) Ancient Greek Πλούτων (Ploútōn)bor. Latin Plūtōbor.

doomsday.e: From Middle English domes + dai, from Old English dom (“judgment”) + dæg (“day”). Equivalent to doom + -s- + day. Compare Old Norse dómsdagr (“judgement day, doomsday”).

moriarty.e: From Irish Ó Muircheartaigh (“descendant of Muircheartach”), a name from muir (“sea”) + ceardaí (“craftsman”).

cougar.e: From French couguar, from Portuguese cuguardo, a deformation of Brazilian Portuguese suçuarana (earlier çuçuarana), from Old Tupi sûasuarana.

guillaume.e: From French. Doublet of Guillermo, William, and Wilhelm, etc.

spaniard.e: From Middle English Spaignarde, from Old French Espaignard, from Espaigne. Equivalent to Spain + -ard.

asparagus.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin asparagus, sparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos), variant of ἀσφάραγος (aspháragos). Displaced Old English eorþnafola. Later became an eggcorn in dialect as sparrowgrass.

quagmire.e: Recorded since 1579, from quag + mire. The sense “perilous, mixed up and troubled situation” has been recorded since 1775.

thorpe.e: Various places in England, from Old English þorp. See also thorpe.

donnelly.e: From the Irish surname, from Ó Donnghaile (“descendant of Donnghal”), from donn (“brown-haired”) + gal (“valor”).

sims.e: From Sim, the short form of Simon + -s.

blasphemy.e: From Middle English blasfemie, from Old French blasfemie, from Ecclesiastical Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”), from βλασφημέω (blasphēméō, “to slander”).

continually.e: Etymology tree English continual Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder.

nu.e: From Ancient Greek νῦ (nû), name for the letter of the Greek alphabet Ν (N) and ν (n).
