loch.e: From Middle English lough, borrowed from Scottish Gaelic loch. Doublet of lay, Looe, and lough.

nudity.e: From nude + -ity. Compare Late Latin nūditās.

spokesman.e: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + man.

itinerary.e: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

monsoon.e: Borrowed from Portuguese monção and Dutch moesson, from Arabic مَوْسِم (mawsim, “season”), from وَسَمَ (wasama, “to mark, to brand”).

unfold.e: From Middle English unfolden, from Old English unfealdan (“to unfold”), equivalent to un- + fold.

appetizer.e: Etymology tree English appetize Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

scripture.e: From Latin scrīptūra (“a writing, scripture”), from scrīptum, the supine of scrībō (“to write”).

relaxation.e: Borrowed from Latin relaxatio, relaxationis; equivalent to relax + -ation.

pox.e: From the plural of Middle English pocke. See also pock. The curse sense involves metonymy: wishing a literal pox upon someone is the original form of pox-relevant curse, and the word pox itself also came to mean curse.

pilar.e: Learned borrowing from Latin pilāris, from Latin pilus (“a hair”) + -ar.

rabid.e: Etymology tree Latin rabiō Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin rabidusbor. English rabid From the Latin rabidus, from rabiō (“to rave”).

cackle.e: From Middle English caclen, cakelen, perhaps from Old English *caclian, *cacolian, from Proto-West Germanic *kakulōn, *kakilōn (“to cackle, gaggle, yelp, snarl”), perhaps of imitative origin.

lovable.e: From Middle English lovable, loveable, luffeabill, lufabul, equivalent to love + -able.

señora.e: Etymology tree Spanish señor Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂ Proto-Italic *-ā Latin -a Old Spanish -a Spanish -a Spanish señorabor. English señora Borrowed from Spanish señora.

termination.e: Borrowed from Latin terminationem (accusative of terminatio).

coy.e: From Middle English coy, from Old French coi, earlier quei (“quiet, still”), from Latin qu(i)ētus (“resting, at rest”). Doublet of quit, quiet, quite, and quietus.

insufficient.e: From Middle French insufficient, from Latin insufficiens. See also in- + sufficient.

ceremonial.e: From Middle English cerymonial, from Latin caerimōniālis. Morphologically ceremony + -al or -ial.

malt.e: From Middle English malt, from Old English mealt, from Proto-West Germanic *malt, from Proto-Germanic *maltą (“malt”), from *maltaz (“soft; nesh; weak; squashy; melting”), from Proto-Indo-European *meld-, *mled- (“to cr…

sudan.e: Derived from Arabic سُودَان (sūdān, “black people”), plural of أَسْوَد (ʔaswad).

brewery.e: From Dutch brouwerij (“brewery”), equivalent to brew + -ery. See also brewhouse.

primal.e: Probably partly from Medieval Latin prīmālis, from Latin prīmus (“first”) + -ālis, and partly from prime + -al.

bidder.e: From Middle English bidder, biddere, equivalent to bid + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Bidder, German Bitter.

dormant.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin dormiēns, present participle of dormiō (“to sleep”).

galen.e: From Middle English Galen, from Latin Galēnus, from Ancient Greek Γαληνός (Galēnós), from γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm, tranquillity”).

sabre.e: Borrowed from French sabre, from German Säbel, from Polish szabla, from Hungarian szablya. Cognate with Danish sabel, Russian са́бля (sáblja), Serbo-Croatian сабља, Sicilian sciàbbula.

apt.e: From Old French apte, from Latin aptus (“suitable, fitting”).

louvre.e: Borrowed from French Louvre. More at Louvre Palace.

homosexuality.e: From homosexual + -ity, equivalent to homo- + sexuality and after the model of German Homosexualität, coined by journalist Karl Maria Kertbeny in 1869, and French homosexualité, attested in 1891.

georg.e: From Danish, Estonian, Faroese, German, Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish Georg, from Latin Geōrgius. The slang sense is from Spiders Georg.

solace.e: From Old French solas, from Latin sōlācium (“consolation”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”).

gladiator.e: From Latin gladiātor, from gladius (“sword”). See also English gladius.

foxy.e: From fox + -y. Compare Saterland Frisian fuksich (“foxy”), West Frisian foksich (“foxy”), Dutch vossig (“foxy”), German Low German vossig (“foxy”), German fuchsig (“foxy”).

scuba.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *swé? Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *selbaz Old English self Old English self- Middle English self- English self- Proto-Indo-European *ḱe?

lui.e: Borrowed from Cantonese 雷 (leoi4) or 呂／吕 (leoi5).

kessler.e: Borrowed from German Kessler, Keßler (“kettler, kettle-smith, tinker”). See also Kessel (“kettle”).

fender.e: Etymology tree English fend Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

mag.e: From Mag, a nickname for Margaret.

cannibal.e: Etymology tree Proto-Cariban *kariponader. Spanish caribeder. Spanish caríbalder. Spanish caníbalbor.

chilled.e: From Middle English chilled, chylled, equivalent to chill + -ed.

leopold.e: From Old French Leopold, from Old High German liut (“people”) + bald (“bold”). The first part is sometimes associated by folk etymology with Latin leo (“lion”), as in Leo and Leonard. More at lede, bold.

milwaukee.e: Perhaps from Ojibwe ominowakiing (“gathering place (by the water)”), or an Algonquin word meaning “the good land”.

rightfully.e: From Middle English ryghtefully, equivalent to rightful + -ly.

vandalism.e: Borrowed from French vandalisme, first used by Henri Grégoire to decry the pillage and destruction of art in the course of the French Revolution, in reference to the East Germanic tribe of the Vandals, which looted Rome…

at least.e: From Middle English at leste, from Old English æt lǣstan.

reginald.e: From Latin Reginaldus, Latinization of names deriving from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz.

robotic.e: From robot + -ic. Coined by American science fiction author Isaac Asimov in 1941 in his short story Liar!.

rolf.e: From Old Norse Hrólfr, and from its Old French equivalent, cognates of Rudolph. Brought to England by the Normans, survived in surnames and was revived in the 19th century, partly due to its modern Scandinavian cognate.

kraut.e: From German Kraut (“cabbage”), alluding to the use of cabbage as an ingredient in German cuisine (namely sauerkraut). First use appears c. 1833–1837, but popularized during the First and Second World Wars.

garibaldi.e: The jacket is named after Italian patriot Giuseppe Garibaldi, who wore a red shirt of similar appearance. The biscuit is also named after Garibaldi.

ragged.e: From Middle English ragged, from North Germanic. Compare with Old Norse rǫgvaðr (“tufted”) and Norwegian ragget (“shaggy”).

roma.e: Borrowed from Romani roma, plural of rom (“man, husband, Romani man”).

surplus.e: From Middle English surplus, from Middle French surplus. Compare French surplus.

judo.e: Borrowed from Japanese 柔(じゅう)道(どう) (jūdō, literally “the soft way”).

doctrine.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.

accessible.e: First attested in 1400, from French, from Late Latin accessibilis, from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”), equivalent to access + -ible.

purposely.e: From Middle English purposly; equivalent to purpose + -ly.

sleet.e: From Middle English slete, probably from Old English *slēte, *slȳte, *slīete, from Proto-West Germanic *slautijā, from Proto-Germanic *slautijǭ (“sleet”). Walter W.

yugoslavia.e: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian Jugoslavija, in turn from jug (“south”) and slavija (“Slavia, the land of the Slavs”). Literally, the land of the South Slavs. By surface analysis, Yugoslav + -ia.

ostrich.e: From Middle English ostrich, ostriche, ostryche, ostrige, borrowed from Anglo-Norman ostrige and Old French ostruce, from Vulgar Latin *austruthio, from Latin avis (“bird”) + strūthiō (“ostrich”), from Ancient Greek στρ…

estelle.e: Borrowed from French Estelle, from Occitan estela (“star”), from Latin stēlla. Doublet of étoile, estoile, stella, and stelo. Name of a third century martyr.

oversee.e: From Middle English overseen, ouverseen, from Old English ofersēon (“to observe, oversee; to overlook, neglect”), equivalent to over- + see.

atrocity.e: From Middle French atrocité, from Latin atrōcitās, from atrōx (“terrible, cruel”) + -tās, from āter (“matte black”).

landmark.e: From Middle English *landmark, from Old English landmearc (“boundary”), from Proto-West Germanic *landamarku (“boundary, landmark”). Equivalent to land + mark.

unimaginable.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-West Germanic *un- Old English un- Middle English un- English un- English imagine Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom…

incriminate.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incrīminātus, perfect passive participle of Latin incrīminō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in 1736. By surface analysis, in- + criminate.

fanatic.e: First attested in 1525. Learned borrowing from Latin fānāticus (“of a temple, divinely inspired, frenzied”), from fānum (“temple”). Influenced by French fanatique.

surreal.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Italic *super Latin super Latin super- Old French sur- French sur- Proto-Indo-European *(H)reh₁-der.

sewage.e: From sewer (“system of pipes used to remove human waste and to provide drainage”) + -age or from sew (“to drain or draw off water”) + -age.

ante.e: Learned borrowing from Latin ante (“before”). Doublet of and.

afloat.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Hellenic *ə- Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-)der. English a- English float English afloat From a- + float.

genevieve.e: Borrowed from French Geneviève (patron saint of Paris), from Latin Genovefa, Genoveva, possibly either of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family”) + *wībą (“woman, wife”), or of Celtic orig…

charisma.e: From Ancient Greek χᾰ́ρῐσμᾰ (khắrĭsmă, “grace, favour, gift”), from χᾰρῐ́ζομαι (khărĭ́zomai, “to show favor”), from χᾰ́ρῐς (khắrĭs, “grace”), from the same root χαρ- (khar-) as χαίρω (khaírō, “to be happy”).

sadistic.e: Etymology tree English sadist Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English sadistic From sadist + -ic.

iconic.e: From Late Latin īconicus, from Ancient Greek εἰκονικός (eikonikós). By surface analysis, icon + -ic.

enormously.e: Etymology tree English enormous Middle English -ly English -ly English enormously From enormous + -ly.

constructive.e: From Latin cōnstrūctīvus. By surface analysis, construct + -ive.

inexperienced.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor.

mast.e: From Middle English mast, from Old English mæst (“mast”), from Proto-West Germanic *mast, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz (“mast, sail-pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *mazdos (“pole, mast”).

meade.e: Two main origins: * A variant of Mead, a topographic or occupational surname. * Anglicized form of Irish Midheach, superseded spelling of Míoch (“Meathman, a native of Meath”).

mead.e: From Middle English mede, from Old English medu, from Proto-West Germanic *medu, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey; honey wine”).

illustrious.e: From Latin illūstris (“bright, shining; distinguished, prominent, illustrious”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, to denote possession or presence of a quality in any degree).

declaring.e: From Middle English declaring, declaryng, declaringe, declarynge, equivalent to declare + -ing (gerund ending).

nucleus.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *knuks Latin nux Latin nucleuslbor. English nucleus Learned borrowing from Latin nucleus (“kernel, core”).

whomever.e: From Middle English whomever; equivalent to whom + -ever.

councillor.e: Alteration of counsellor, by assimilation with council. By surface analysis, council + -or.

cowl.e: From Middle English coule, from Old English cūle, from earlier cugele (“hood, cowl”), from Ecclesiastical Latin cuculla (“monk's cowl”), from Latin cucullus (“hood”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of cagoule.

townsend.e: From town + -s- + end. From Middle English toun (“hamlet, village”) + ende (“end”), referring to a dweller at the outskirts of a village.

unsure.e: From Middle English unsure, equivalent to un- + sure. Piecewise doublet of insecure and unsecure.

costello.e: * As an Irish surname, reduced Anglicized form of Irish Mac Oisdealbhaigh (“son of Oisdealbhach”), a personal name composed of the elements os (“deer”) and dealbhach (“resembling, in the form of”).

henrietta.e: Latinate form of French Henriette, derived from the male given name Henry.

marla.e: American back-formation from Marlene, first used in the 1930s.

provocation.e: From Middle English provocacioun, from Old French provocacion, from Late Latin prōvocātiō, prōvocātiōnem, from Latin prōvocō. By surface analysis, provoke + -ation. Doublet of provokatsiya.

perverse.e: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).

nutrient.e: Borrowed from Latin nūtriēns, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).

occult.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁óp(i) Proto-Italic *op Latin ob Latin ob- Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- Proto-Indo-European *ḱéletider.

shawl.e: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi शाल (śāl) / Urdu شال (śāl)), from Classical Persian شال (šāl). Doublet of sari through Sanskrit.

twitch.e: From Middle English twicchen, from Old English *twiċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *twikkijan (“to nail, pin, fasten, clasp, pinch”).

browning.e: From Old English Brūning, a patronymic for a person nicknamed Brūn (“brown”) (see Brown). For the first half-century of their manufacturer, the majority of semi-automatic handguns in Europe were designed by John M.

upward.e: From Old English upweardes, equivalent to up + -ward.

burp.e: Originally from American English, of imitative origin.

ludicrous.e: Learned borrowing from Latin lūdicrus. First attested in 1619.

bridesmaid.e: From bride + -s- + maid. In the sports and entertainment sense: in reference to the saying always a bridesmaid, never a bride.

deployment.e: From French déploiement. Also de- + ployment.

pence.e: Americanized spelling of German Pentz or Benz.

predecessor.e: From Middle English predecessour, from Old French predecesseor (“forebear”), from Late Latin praedēcessor, from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + Latin dēcessor (“retiring officer”), from Latin dēcēdō (“to retire, to die”) (Englis…

tian.e: From French, from Provençal tian, from Old Occitan, from Ancient Greek τήγανον (tḗganon), variant of τάγηνον (tágēnon, “frying pan”).

avon.e: From Proto-Brythonic *aβon (“river”). Compare with Welsh afon. Doublet of Almond (“a river in Scotland”).

blowjob.e: First used in the USA. From blow off (“to fellate”, originating among prostitutes from 1933) + job.

ashton.e: From Old English æsc (“ash (tree species)”) + tūn (“enclosure, settlement”).

blockade.e: From block + -ade, probably after Dutch blocquade (now blokkade) or German Blockade.

mischievous.e: From Middle English myschevous, mischevous, from Anglo-Norman meschevous, from Old French meschever, from mes- (“mis-”) + chever (“come to an end”) (from chef (“head”)). By surface analysis, mischief + -ous.

jiffy.e: Origin unknown; said to have been thieves’ cant for “lightning”. Also formerly written "giffy", to which a connection with gliff has been proposed. As a kind of envelope, a genericization of Jiffy bag.

repressed.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English press English repress English -ed English repressed From repress + -ed.

driscoll.e: From Irish Ó hEidirsceoil and Ó Drisceoil.

yarn.e: From Middle English yern, yarn, from the Old English ġearn (“yarn, spun wool”), from Proto-West Germanic *garn, from Proto-Germanic *garną (“yarn”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰorn-, *ǵʰerH- (“tharm, guts, intestines”).

catchy.e: Etymology tree substratebor.? Proto-Indo-European *kap- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *kapyéti Proto-Indo-European *kaptós Proto-Italic *kaptos Latin captus Proto-Indo-European *-yetider.

deserter.e: Borrowed from Latin desertor (“deserter”), from desero (“to forsake, to abandon”); or from desert + -er.

documentation.e: From document + -ation or Medieval Latin documentātio.

hotch.e: From Anglo-Norman hocher, Middle French hocher, from a Germanic source (compare Dutch hutsen, hossen, German hotzen).

dunham.e: Habitational surname from any of various places in England, from Old English dūn (“hill”) + hām (“homestead”).

playoff.e: Deverbal from play off; by surface analysis, play + -off.

feisty.e: First use appears c. 1875 in the US.

plainly.e: From Middle English playnly, pleinly, pleyneliche, equivalent to plain + -ly.

federico.e: Borrowed from Italian Federico (through immigration). Doublet of Frederick.

highlands.e: Specific application of highlands, equivalent to high + lands.

hustler.e: Etymology tree English hustle Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

paternity.e: From Middle French paternité, from Old French, from Latin paternitās (“paternity”), from paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).

washer.e: From Middle English wasshere, wassher, equivalent to wash + -er. Cognate with Dutch wasser, German Wäscher.

borne.e: From Middle English boren, iborne, from Old English boren, ġeboren, past participle of Old English beran (“to carry, bear”).

disclosure.e: From disclose by analogy with closure. A purely English formation.

indigestion.e: From Middle English indigestioun, from Old French indigestion, from Late Latin indigestio, by surface analysis, in- + digestion.

spur.e: From Middle English spure, spore, from Old English spora, spura, from Proto-West Germanic *spurō, from Proto-Germanic *spurô, from Proto-Indo-European *sperH- (“to kick”).

cabe.e: Reduced form of MacCabe or McCabe, anglicized form of Irish Mac Cába.

mayer.e: * As an English surname, variant of Mear, from the noun mere (both senses). * Also as an English surname, from Middle English mire, a borrowing from archaic French mire (“physician”). Compare Myer.

renegade.e: From Spanish renegado, from Medieval Latin renegātus, perfect participle of renegō (“to deny”). See also renege.

barley.e: From Middle English barly, barli, from Old English bærlīċ (“barley-like”, adjective) (later referring to barley itself and grain crops of similar appearance), from bere (“barley”) (compare Scots bere (“six-rowed barley”…

inquest.e: From Middle English enquest, from Old French enqueste (Modern French enquête), from Vulgar Latin inquirere, or from Medieval Latin inquesta < in + Latin quaesita.

humidity.e: From Middle English humidite, borrowed from Old French humidité, from Medieval Latin hūmiditās, from Latin ūmidus (“damp, moist, wet”). By surface analysis, humid + -ity.

priscilla.e: Feminine diminutive form of a Roman cognomen Prīscus, from Latin prīscus (“former, ancient, old-fashioned”). Compare typologically Seneca (< Latin Seneca < senex).

mythical.e: From Latin mȳthicus + -al; by surface analysis, myth + -ical.

paramount.e: PIE word *h₂éd From Anglo-Norman paramont /paramount (“paramount, pre-eminent; above”), from Old French par /per (“by”) + amont /amunt (“upward”).

neatly.e: Etymology tree English neat Middle English -ly English -ly English neatly From neat + -ly.

volvo.e: From Swedish Volvo, from Latin volvō (“to roll”), in reference to ball bearings which were the company's original product.

frivolous.e: From Latin frīvolus (“silly, empty, trifling, frivolous, worthless”), with the ending modified to match -ous.

duly.e: From Middle English duely, dewly, dulyche, dueliche, duweliche (“rightly, properly”), equivalent to due + -ly.

glide.e: From Middle English gliden, from Old English glīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰleydʰ-.

nameless.e: From Middle English nameles, equivalent to name + -less.

armando.e: Borrowed from Italian, Portuguese and Spanish Armando.

electron.e: Blend of electric + ion, coined by Anglo-Irish scientist George Stoney in 1891, changed by him multiple times from an earlier electrolion and original electrine (used as early as 1874) as the name for the electric charg…

howe.e: * As an English surname, from Middle English hoʒe (“steep ridge”), a late variant of hōge, dative case of Old English hoh (“hock, heel”), with likely influence from Old Norse haugr (“hill”).

sketchy.e: From sketch + -y. Extension of "brief, imperfect, unfinished" notion.

malice.e: From Middle English malice, borrowed from Old French malice, from Latin malitia (“badness, bad quality, ill-will, spite”), from malus (“bad”).

billing.e: From the Old English surname, named after Billing in Liverpool, from bil (“double-edged sword”).

cornwall.e: From Middle English Cornwaile, Cornwayle, a modification of Cornwale (after Old French Cornuaille), from Old English Cornwēalas (“Cornwall, inhabitants of Cornwall”), from Proto-Celtic *kornu (“horn”) + Old English weal…

crusher.e: From crush + -er (agent noun suffix), or, for one who elicits a crush, + -er (patient suffix).

reinforced.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English inforce English reinforce English -ed English reinforced From reinforce + -ed.

reinforce.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re-bor. Middle English re- English re- English inforce English reinforce From re- + inforce.

yamada.e: Borrowed from Japanese 山(やま)田(だ) (Yamada).

newark.e: Probably from Old English nīewe (“new”) + weorc (“work”). In this case, a perhaps more accurate sense of "work" would be that of a building, as an example of a work of labor.

janis.e: A variant of Janice. Doublet of Ivana, Jana, Janice, Jean, Jeanne, Jen, Joan, Joanna, Joanne, Johanna, Juana, Shavonne, Sian, Siobhan, Shane, Shaun, Shauna, and Sheena.

provocative.e: Borrowed from Middle French provocatif, and its source, Late Latin provocativus, from Latin provocare.

complimentary.e: From compliment (noun) + -ary. Piecewise doublet of complementary.

bethlehem.e: Inherited from Middle English Bethleem, from Old French Bethleem and Old English Bethleem, from Latin Bēthlehēmum, from Ancient Greek Βηθλεέμ (Bēthleém), from Hebrew בֵּית לֶחֶם (bēṯ lɛ́ḥɛm, literally “house of bread”).

bordeaux.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃-der. Proto-Celtic *bitus? Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs Proto-Celtic *rīxs? Gaulish Biturīgesder.

festivity.e: Inherited from Middle English festivite, from Middle French festivité, from Latin festīvitas, equivalent to festive + -ity.

migration.e: From Middle French migration and its source, Latin migrātiō, from the participle stem of migrō (“to migrate”). Morphologically migrate + -ion.

brig.e: Abbreviated from brigantine, from Italian brigantino; in sense “jail”, from the use of such ships as prisons.

distraught.e: From Middle English distraught, blend of distract (“distracted”) and straught (“stretched, distraught”), past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”). Compare also bestraught, extraught, forstraught, etc.

grasshopper.e: From Middle English grashoppere, alteration of earlier grashoppe, from Old English græshoppa (“grasshopper”). Equivalent to grass + hopper.

ashok.e: Borrowed from Hindi अशोक (aśok), from Sanskrit अशोक (aśoka, literally “without grief”). Doublet of Ashoka and Asoka.

desolate.e: From Middle English desolat(e). See Etymology 2 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

masturbation.e: Borrowed from French masturbation, New Latin masturbātiō, masturbātiōnem. By surface analysis, masturbat(e) + -ion.

fiasco.e: Borrowed from Italian fiasco (“bottle, flask”), from Late Latin flasca, flascō (“bottle, container”), from Frankish *flaskā (“bottle, flask”) from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”); see flask.

kung fu.e: From the Wade–Giles romanization of Mandarin 功夫 (gōngfu, “skill, accomplishment, martial art”): kung¹-fu⁵.

sufficiently.e: Etymology tree English sufficient Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder.

hereditary.e: Inherited from Middle English hereditarie, from Latin hērēditārius, from hērēditās (“inheritance”), from hērēs (“heir”).

psychologically.e: Etymology tree English psychology Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor.

falsely.e: From Middle English falsly, falsliche, equivalent to false + -ly.

brightly.e: From Middle English brightliche, from Old English beorhtlice, equivalent to bright + -ly.

rosario.e: From Spanish rosario (“rosary”). Doublet of rosarium and rosary.

envoy.e: From French envoyé (“envoy, messenger”), from envoyer (“send”).

tia.e: Invented in the latter half of the twentieth century. It can be explained as a short form of Letitia or Venetia, or from Estonian Tiia, pet form of Dorothea.

improper.e: From Middle French impropre, from Latin improprius (“not proper”), from in- + proprius (“proper”). By surface analysis, im- + proper.

niagara.e: From an Iroquoian language; compare Mohawk ohnyá:kara' (“neck of land”). The name of the tribe which resided in the area was recorded on early maps as Onguiarahronon or Niagagarega.

highland.e: From Middle English hy laund, holond (“highland, upland”), from Old English hēahland (“highland”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauhaland, *hauhalandī; equivalent to high + land.

terence.e: From Latin Terentius, a Roman family name of obscure origin, borne by a Roman playwright and by early Christian saints. * In Ireland, it has been used to represent Turlough.

honorary.e: From honor + -ary, modelled after French honoraire, from Latin honōrārius.

concession.e: From late Middle English concession, from Middle French concession, from Latin concessiō (“a grant, permission, conceding”), from concēdō. Doublet of concessio.

nutrition.e: Borrowed from Middle French nutrition, from Old French nutricion, from Latin nutritio.

kendra.e: Coined in the latter half of the twentieth century, presumably a blend of Kenneth + Sandra.

olympus.e: From Latin Olympus, from Ancient Greek Ὄλυμπος (Ólumpos), likely of Pre-Greek origin.

unison.e: Since 1993. Created as a play on unison, as the united workers act in unison.

ion.e: From the ending of anion and cation, which in turn is from Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión, “going”), neuter present participle of εἶμι (eîmi, “I go”).

bozo.e: Attested since the 1910s in American English, of uncertain origin. The term may derive from Spanish bozal, a term originally for a recently-imported slave and then "someone who speaks (Spanish) poorly".

undertake.e: From Middle English undertaken; equivalent to under- + take (after undernim).

sprout.e: From Middle English sproute, either from Middle English sprouten (“to sprout”) (see below); or from Middle Dutch sprute or Middle Low German sprûte (“sprout”), all related to Proto-West Germanic *spreutan.

irwin.e: From a medieval given name Erwin, from Eoforwine, from Old English eofor (“boar”) + wine (“friend”), the latter of which is from Proto-West Germanic *wini.

fink.e: Unknown; first attested in 1894. A connection to Yiddish as some propose is unlikely.

visionary.e: Etymology tree Middle English visioun English vision Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusder. Middle English -arie English -ary English visionary From vision + -ary.

talkative.e: From Middle English talkatyve, equivalent to talk + -ative.

alyssa.e: A 20th-century invention. Possible origins: * From alyss(um) (“a plant of the genus Alyssum”) + -a. * From Alicia, of Germanic origin. * From Elissa.

sie.e: From Middle English sien, from Old English sīgan (“to sink, descend”), from Proto-Germanic *sīganą, *sīhwaną (“to strain, drop”), from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“to pour, strain”).

kemp.e: From Middle English kempe (“coarse hairs”), from Old English cenep (“moustache; bit (of a bridle, bristling with points)”), from Proto-West Germanic *kanip, from Proto-Germanic *kanipaz (“beard, moustache, whiskers”), f…

unkind.e: Inherited from Middle English unkynde; equivalent to un- + kind.

conservation.e: From Old French. By surface analysis, conserve + -ation.

valeria.e: Feminine form of Roman family name Valerius, from Latin valere (“to be healthy, to be strong”). Doublet of Valerie.

diabolical.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ ▲ Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Proto-Indo-European *dwísder. Ancient Greek διά (diá) Ancient Greek δια- (dia-) Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-der.

breather.e: From breathe + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (relational noun suffix).

profoundly.e: From Middle English profoundly, profoundely, equivalent to profound + -ly.

hester.e: From the Latin form of Esther.

cantonese.e: Etymology tree English Canton Proto-Indo-European *-iskos Proto-Germanic *-iskaz Proto-West Germanic *-iskbor. Late Latin -iscus ▲ Vulgar Latin -iscus Latin -ēnsis Old French -eisbor.

pika.e: From French, from an Evenki word which Peter Simon Pallas transcribes as piika or peeka, but which cannot be found in modern dictionaries. Probably ultimately onomatopoeic.

martina.e: Usually interpreted as the feminine form of the saints' name Martin, though there was an identical Roman name, likewise derived from Latin Martinus.

clarkson.e: From Middle English clerc (“cleric”) + -son, equivalent to Clark + -son.

outright.e: From Middle English outright. By surface analysis, out + right.

ito.e: Borrowed from Japanese 伊藤 (Itō) or Japanese 伊東 (Itō).

downward.e: Etymology tree English down Proto-Indo-European *wert-der. Proto-Germanic *wardaz Old English -weard English -ward English downward From down + -ward.

okinawa.e: Borrowed from Japanese 沖縄(おきなわ) (Okinawa).

palate.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂-? Proto-Indo-European *pel-? Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-osder. Latin palātumder. Old French palatbor.

nakamura.e: Borrowed from Japanese 中村 (Nakamura) or 仲村 (Nakamura).

emmet.e: ), but probably from Proto-Germanic *ē- (“off, away”) + *maitaną (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂y- (“to cut”). Doublet of ant.

nasal.e: From Middle English, from Medieval Latin nāsālis, from nāsus (“the nose”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of nasalis.

winged.e: From Middle English winged, wenged (“having wings”), past participle of wingen, from the noun winge, wenge.

bernice.e: Biblical form of Berenice, from Ancient Greek Βερενίκη (Bereníkē).

musketeer.e: From Middle French mousquetaire in the late 16th century. By surface analysis, musket + -eer. Doublet of mousquetaire.

tumour.e: From Middle English tumour, from Old French tumour, from Latin tumor (“swelling”), from tumeō (“bulge, swell”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”). Related to English thumb.

stature.e: From Middle English stature, from Old French stature, from Latin statūra.

lakshmi.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂lek- Sanskrit रक्ष् (rakṣ)? Sanskrit लक्ष् (lakṣ) Sanskrit लक्ष्मी (lakṣmī)bor. English Lakshmi Borrowed from Sanskrit लक्ष्मी (lakṣmī, “mark, sign”).

eunice.e: A biblical name from Ancient Greek Εὐνίκη (Euníkē), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + νίκη (níkē, “victory”).

attentive.e: From Middle English attentif, attentijf, from Old French attentif.

dunbar.e: Historically Dynbaer. From Cumbric *dyn (“fort”) + *barr (“hill-crest, summit, top”).

equity.e: From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

ringer.e: From Middle English ringere, rynger, ryngar, equivalent to ring (“to sound a bell”) + -er.

delinquent.e: Borrowed from Middle French délinquant, ultimately from Latin delinquens, present participle of delinquo.

schizophrenia.e: From German Schizophrenie (coined by Eugen Bleuler), from Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”) + φρήν (phrḗn, “mind, heart, diaphragm”) + English -ia. A combination of schizo- + -phrenia.

sculptor.e: Borrowed from Latin sculptor, equivalent to sculpt + -or.

netherlands.e: From nether (“lower”) + lands, the country being very low-lying, with a great part below sea level. Either a calque or a parallel formation to Dutch Nederland.

inca.e: Borrowed from Spanish inca, from Classical Quechua inka (“emperor”).

ado.e: From Northern Middle English at do (“to do”), infinitive of do, don (“to do”), see do. Influenced by an Old Norse practice of marking the infinitive by using the preposition at, att (compare Danish at gå (“to go”)).

odessa.e: Borrowed from Russian Оде́сса (Odéssa), named after an Ancient Greek settlement thought to have been located nearby. Ancient Greek Ὀδησσός (Odēssós). Compare Ukrainian Оде́са (Odésa).

neurological.e: Etymology tree English neurology Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor.

guerrilla.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *wers-der. Proto-Germanic *werzaną Proto-West Germanic *werʀan Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Germanic *-ō Proto-West Germanic *-u Frankish *werʀubor.

charismatic.e: From Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma, “grace, favour, gift”) + -ic.

garret.e: From Middle English garett, garite, from Old French garite, guerite (“watchtower”), from garir, guarir (“to defend, protect”) (compare English garrison), ultimately of Germanic origin (see English garage).

funnel.e: From Middle English funell, fonel, probably through Old French *founel (compare Middle French fonel, Old Occitan fonilh, enfounilh), from Latin fundibulum, infundibulum (“funnel”), from infundere (“to pour in”); in (“in…

curator.e: From Latin cūrātor (“one who has care of a thing, a manager, guardian, trustee”), from cūrāre (“to take care of”), from cūra (“care, heed, attention, anxiety, grief”).

himalayas.e: Pluralisation of Himalaya, learned borrowing from Sanskrit हिमालय (himālaya).

tulip.e: From Middle French tulipe, from earlier tulipan, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (tülbent, dülbent, “cheesecloth”), from Classical Persian دلبند (dulband, “turban”). Doublet of turban.

sharpen.e: From Middle English scharpenen, scharpnen, equivalent to sharp + -en.

hathaway.e: Two possible origins: * A topographic surname for someone who lived by a path across a heath, from Old English hǣþ (“heath, untilled land”) + weġ (“way”).

reconciliation.e: From Middle English reconciliacioun (“act of reconciling; state of accord or harmony;”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman reconciliaciun, reconsiliacion, reconsiliaciun, and Middle French reconciliation, reconsiliaci…

greenwich.e: From Middle English Greenwich, from Old English Grēnawīċ, Grēnewīċ (literally “green harbour, green settlement”). Equivalent to green + -wich.

waterloo.e: From Middle Dutch, composed of water (“water”) + loo (“sacred wood, forest”). More at water, lea. cf. German Loh. Most places in English-speaking countries are named for the battle.

isaiah.e: From Ancient Greek Ἠσαΐας (Ēsaḯas) from Hebrew יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (yəšaʿyā́hū).

induce.e: From Middle English enducen, borrowed from Latin indūcere (“lead in, bring in, introduce”), from in + dūcō (“lead, conduct”). Compare also abduce, adduce, conduce, deduce, produce, reduce etc. Doublet of endue.

cortez.e: From Spanish Cortez, variant of Cortés.

wasteland.e: Inherited from Middle English wast lond, modification of earlier weste lond, from Old English weste land (“wasteland”); equivalent to waste + land.

smokey.e: Short for Smokey Bear (“a cartoon Park Ranger”).

smoky.e: From Middle English smoke, smokei, smoki, smokie, smoky, equivalent to smoke + -y (adjectival suffix). Doublet of Samoki.

nostalgic.e: Etymology tree Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos) Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos) New Latin nostalgiabor. English nostalgia Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor.

longitude.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French longitude, from Latin longitūdō (“length, a measured length”), from longus (“long”).

leprechaun.e: From Irish leipreachán, luprachán, from Middle Irish luchrupán, from Old Irish luchorpán. See also Irish lucharachán.

analogy.e: From Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογίᾱ (analogíā), from ἀνα- (ana-) + λόγος (lógos, “speech, reckoning”).

levine.e: Borrowed from French Levine, from Russian Левин (Levin), from Леви (Levi) + -ин (-in, “forming possessives & adjectives”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (“Levi”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levin.

nightgown.e: From Middle English nyght gowne. By surface analysis, night + gown.

demolish.e: Attested since the 16th century; from Middle French demoliss-, the stem of some conjugated forms of the verb demolir (“to destroy”, “to tear down”), from Latin dēmōlior (“to tear down”).

lafayette.e: French surname from Occitan, "the little beech tree".

vigilant.e: From French vigilant or its source, Latin vigilans, present participle of vigilare (“stay awake”), from vigil (“awake”). Doublet of vigilante, from Spanish. Displaced Old English wacor.

withhold.e: From Middle English withholden. Equivalent to with- + hold.

burnett.e: From Middle English burnet (“brown”), from Old French brunet, brunete.

grapefruit.e: Widely assumed to be a marketing term from grape + fruit, an allusion to the supposed grapelike clusters of fruit on the tree, early 19th c.

deodorant.e: From Latin de- + odorans, present participle of odorare (“to smell”), from odor (“a smell”); see odor. By surface analysis, de- + odor + -ant.

remnant.e: From Middle English, contraction of remenant, from Anglo-Norman remanant, present participle of remaindre, from Latin remaneō.

nachos.e: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish nachos, from Nacho. Nacho is a common diminutive form of Ignacio (“Ignatius”) in Spanish.

munition.e: From Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”) via French munition, from mūnīre (“fortify, defend (with a wall)”) + -tiō, from moenia (“city walls, defensive walls, or walls in general”). Equivalent to munite + -ion.

rochelle.e: Habitational or topographic name from places in France, La Rochelle, from Old French rochelle diminutive form of roche (“rock”).

twain.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Germanic *twai Proto-West Germanic *twai-der.

acceleration.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- Proto-Indo-European *kel-der.

surya.e: Borrowed from Sanskrit सूर्य (sū́rya, “the sun or its deity”). Doublet of sun.

seduction.e: Borrowed from Middle French séduction, from Latin sēductiō, from sēdūcō. Equivalent to seduce + -tion.

ezekiel.e: From Koine Greek Ἰεζεκιήλ (Iezekiḗl), from Biblical Hebrew יְחֶזְקֵאל (Y'ḥezqēl, “God strengthens”).

hazardous.e: From Middle French hasardeux, equivalent to hazard + -ous.

collide.e: From Latin collīdō (“to clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together”), from con- (“together”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence col- (“assimilated form of com-”)).

iphone.e: From i- + phone. Many Apple products have an i- prefix in their names.

porky.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *perḱ- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos Proto-Italic *porkos Latin porcus Old French porcbor.

revoke.e: Borrowed from Middle French révoquer, from Latin revocare, from re- + voco, vocare. Doublet of revocate.

cinematography.e: From cinematograph + -y. Compare French cinématographie. Possibly analysable as cinemato- + -graphy.

variation.e: From Middle French variation, from Old French variacion, from Latin variātiō, from vary + -ation.

asa.e: ZU /⁠azu⁠/, “physician, healer”); compare Classical Syriac ܐܵܣܝܵܐ (ʾāsyā, “healer, physician, medical doctor”) whence Arabic آسٍ (ʔāsin).

abode.e: From Middle English abod, abad, from Old English *ābād, related to ābīdan (“to abide”); see abide. Cognate with Scots abade, abaid (“abode”). For the change of nouns, compare abode, preterite of abide.

elmer.e: Medieval variant of the given name Aylmer, from Old English Æþelmǣr, from æþel (“noble”) + mǣre (“famous”).

latitude.e: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French latitude, from Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus. Possibly related with lateral, though this is uncertain.

salazar.e: From Spanish Salazar, from archaic Basque Sarasaitzu (modern Zaraitzu).

clarice.e: Borrowed from French Clarisse, from Italian Clarissa, from Medieval Latin Clarissa (“Poor Clare”); see there for more. Doublet of Clarissa and Clarisse.

sledge.e: From Middle English slegge, from Old English sleċġ (“sledgehammer; mallet”), from Proto-Germanic *slagjǭ.

shrewd.e: From Middle English schrewed (“depraved; wicked”, literally “accursed”), from schrewen (“to curse; beshrew”), from schrewe, schrowe, screwe (“evil or wicked person/thing”), from Old English sċrēawa (“wicked person”, lit…

spatter.e: Probably from Middle Low German or Dutch spatten (“to spout, burst”) + -er (frequentative suffix). Related to spit (“saliva”).

nostril.e: From Middle English nostrille, from Old English nosþyrel. Compare Old Frisian nosterle (“nostril”), modern West Frisian noaster (“nostrill”).

fillet.e: From Middle English filet, vylette, felet, filette, flette, from Old French filet, diminutive of fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).

locally.e: Etymology tree English local Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder.

consistently.e: Etymology tree English consistent Middle English -ly English -ly English consistently From consistent + -ly.

u-turn.e: From U + turn, from the similarity to the shape of the letter U.

tres.e: Borrowed from Spanish tres (“three”). Doublet of three and trey.

bumblebee.e: 1520s from bumble + bee, replacing Middle English humbul-be. Merged with Middle English bombeln (“to boom, buzz”), in the late 14th century. The name of the drink is a semantic loan from Ukrainian джміль (džmilʹ).

mccall.e: Anglicized form of Gaelic Mac Cathail ("son of Cathal").

annabel.e: Originally a mishearing or misreading of Latin amabilis (“lovable”) (= Amabel, Mabel), used since the 12th century and by folk etymology interpreted as Anna + belle, "beautiful Anna".

visualize.e: From visual + -ize (suffix forming verbs denoting the doing or making of what is denoted by the adjectives or nouns to which it is attached).

juggling.e: From Middle English jogelyng, juglynge, equivalent to juggle + -ing.

beige.e: Unadapted borrowing from French (dialectal) beige, from Old French bege (“color of undyed wool or cotton”), from an Alpine language (compare Franco-Provençal bézho, Romansch besch (“dull grey”)), from Vulgar Latin *byss…

oslo.e: From Norwegian Oslo, from Old Norse Ósló, Ásló f or n. The first element is disputed, but is likely from ǫ́ss, áss (“god; one of the Æsir”), from Proto-Germanic *ansuz.

enigma.e: From Latin aenigma (“riddle”), being derived itself from the Ancient Greek verbal noun αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, speaking in riddles”).

marseilles.e: From Old French Marseilles (nominative of Marseille), from Latin Massilia, Marsilia, from Ancient Greek Μασσαλία (Massalía), probably from a pre-Latin language of Italy, perhaps Ancient Ligurian mas (“spring”).

memento.e: Borrowed from Latin mementō (“remember”), imperative form of meminī (“to remember”).

bedford.e: From Middle English Bedforde, Bedeford, from Old English Bedaford, Bedanford, equivalent to Bede's + ford. The civil parish is named after John Russell, 4th Duke of Bedford (1710 - 1771).

contraband.e: From Spanish contrabanda (modern spelling contrabando), from Italian contrabando (modern spelling contrabbando), from contra (“against”) + bando (“ban”), and reinforced by French contrebande.

albanian.e: From Albania + -n. Doublet of Albanese. Compare Middle French Albanien and old Albanian endonym arbën, arbër (“Albanian”).

ravine.e: Borrowed from French ravin (“a gully”), from Old French raviner (“to pillage, sweep down, cascade”), from ravine (“robbery, rapine; violent rush of water, waterfall, avalanche; impetuosity, spirit”), from Latin rapīna (…

protester.e: Etymology tree English protest Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

writ.e: From Middle English writ, from Old English writ and ġewrit (“writing”), from Proto-Germanic *writą (“fissure, writing”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey-, *wrī- (“to scratch, carve, ingrave”).

heroism.e: From French héroïsme, equivalent to hero + -ism.

prolong.e: Either a back-formation from prolongation, or from Old French prolonguer or porloignier, from Latin prōlongō, from prō + longō. Doublet of purloin.

benevolent.e: From Old French benevolent, borrowed from Latin benevolēns ("benevolent"). Displaced native Old English welwillende (literally well-wishing).

nutcase.e: From nut + case. Compare headcase, mental case etc.

deity.e: From Middle French deité, from Latin deitās.

quebec.e: From French Québec, from Algonquin kepék (“(it) narrows”). Cognate with Mi'kmaq gepe'g (“plug”), and Mi'kmaq Kepinkek.

unnie.e: Borrowed from Korean 언니 (eonni, “older sister of a woman”).

rodent.e: From Latin rōdēns, rōdent- (“gnawer; one who gnaws”), present participle of rōdō (“to gnaw”).

schwartz.e: Borrowed from German Schwartz. Doublet of Swart.

tyrone.e: From Irish Tír Eoghain (literally “land of Eoghan”).

vamoose.e: Alteration of Spanish vamos (“we go”) or vámonos (“let's go”). Doublet of namous.

benign.e: From Middle English benigne, benygne, from Old French benigne, from Latin benignus (“kind, good”), from bene (“well”) + genus (“origin, kind”). Compare malign.

charmer.e: From Middle English charmer, charmere, equivalent to charm + -er.

gnome.e: From French gnome (“gnome”), from New Latin gnomus, used by Paracelsus as a synonym for pygmaeus (“pygmy”).

miley.e: Popularised as a female name by American pop singer Miley Ray Cyrus (nicknamed Miley from "smiley").

kebab.e: Ultimately from Arabic كَبَاب (kabāb), partly through Hindustani (Hindi and Urdu), Punjabi, Persian and Turkish kebap. Doublet of cevapi. See the Arabic entry for more.

redundant.e: From Latin redundāns, present participle of redundō (“to overflow, redound”), from red- (“again, back”) + undō (“to surge, flood”), from unda (“a wave”).

yusuf.e: Borrowed from Arabic يُوسُف (yūsuf), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹסֵף (yoséf). Doublet of Joseph.

celtic.e: Borrowed from French celtique or Latin celticus, equivalent to Celt + -ic. First attested in the 17th century.

superiority.e: From Middle English superiorite, from Old French superiorite, from Medieval Latin superioritas, from Latin superior. Morphologically superior + -ity.

holloway.e: From Old English holh (“hollow”) + weġ (“way”); compare the doublet Holway.

nightly.e: From Middle English nyȝtly, nihtlich, nihtlic, from Old English nihtlīċ, nihtelīċ (“nocturnal, nightly, of the night, at night”), equivalent to night + -ly.

varsity.e: First attested in the mid-17th century. Clipping of univarsity, reflecting an archaic pronunciation of university.

damascus.e: From Latin Dāmascus, from Ancient Greek Δαμασκός (Damaskós), from a Semitic form akin to Hebrew דַּמֶּשֶׂק and Samalian 𐤃𐤌𐤔𐤒 (dmšq). Doublet of Dimashq.

digestive.e: From Old French digestif, from Late Latin dīgestīvus. Doublet of digestif.

deficit.e: From French déficit, from Latin dēficit. Related to defect.

barrister.e: From bar (a collective term for lawyers or the legal profession) and the suffix -ster.

doggone.e: Minced oath of goddamn or goddamned.

christening.e: From Middle English cristenynge, from Old English cristnung; compare christen + -ing.

gothic.e: From Late Latin gothicus (“Gothic, barbaric”), from Ancient Greek Γοτθικός (Gotthikós), from Ancient Greek Γότθοι (Gótthoi, “Goths”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”), proposed to derive from unattested Gothic *𐌲𐌿𐍄𐌰 (*guta).

ethiopia.e: From Latin Aethiopia, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπία (Aithiopía), from Αἰθίοψ (Aithíops), of Proto-Hellenic origin. Displaced native Old English Siġelhearwena land (literally “land of the sun worshippers”).

shroud.e: From Middle English shroud, from Old English sċrūd, from Proto-Germanic *skrūdą (“shroud, dress, attire”). Compare Proto-Germanic *skrūdijaną (“to shroud”).

dingo.e: Borrowed from Dharug dingu (“tame or domesticated dingo”).

betrothed.e: From Middle English, equivalent to betroth + -ed.

justification.e: From Middle English justificacioun, justification, from Middle French justification, from Late Latin iustificationem, justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from Latin iustus.

conqueror.e: From Middle English conquerour, from Old French conquereor, from conquerre. By surface analysis, conquer + -or.

favourable.e: From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favour + -able.

bonkers.e: Unknown. Perhaps from bonk (a blow or punch on the head, compare whacky); perhaps related to earlier bonce.

jest.e: From Middle English geste (“idle tale”), from Old French geste (“acts, exploits”), from Latin gesta (“acts, deeds”). Doublet of gest.

toddler.e: From toddle (“to walk unsteadily”) + -er – literally “one who walks unsteadily”, hence a young child.

lager.e: From German Lagerbier (“beer made for storing”), from Lager (“store”). Cognate with native English lair.

septic.e: From Ancient Greek σηπτικός (sēptikós, “characterized by putridity”), from σηπτός (sēptós), from σήπω (sḗpō).

graces.e: From Latin Gratiae, from gratia (“grace”), from Ancient Greek χᾰ́ρῐς (khắrĭs, “grace, charity”).

mueller.e: From German Müller (“miller”). Doublet of Miller.

avocado.e: Borrowed from Latin American Spanish avocado, from the earlier aguacate, which comes from Classical Nahuatl āhuacatl (“avocado”). Doublet of abacate. Compare aguacatillo, avocadillo.

oaf.e: Variant of awf, aufe, probably from Old Norse álfr (“elf”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål alv). Doublet of alf and elf.

corbett.e: From Anglo-Norman corbet (“little crow; carrion crow”), probably a nickname for someone with dark hair or complexion.

flex.e: From Latin flexus, past participle of flecto (“to bend”).

danes.e: Various origins: * Patronymic or genitive form of Dane, a variant of Dean. * Borrowed from Dutch Danes, a short form of the personal name Daniel. * Borrowed from Czech and Slovak Daneš.

silky.e: From Middle English sylky, equivalent to silk + -y.

popsicle.e: Blend of pop (“father”) + Epsicle, from Epperson + icicle. Named after Frank Epperson, its inventor. The inventor's children renamed it Popsicle, from Pop's 'sicle.

yau.e: From Hokkien 姚 (Iâu), Cantonese 丘 (jau1), Cantonese 邱 (jau1), Cantonese 尤 (jau4), Cantonese 游 (jau4), etc.

encyclopedia.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁én Ancient Greek ἐν (en) Ancient Greek ἐν- (en-) Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-redup.

stationary.e: From Latin stationarius, from statio, ultimately from stō (“to stand”). Doublet of stationer.

dink.e: Imitative. Originally US. Attested since the 1930s.

guinness.e: An Anglicization of Irish Mac Aonghusa (literally “son of Angus”).

excruciating.e: Present participle of excruciate, from Latin excruciō, from ex- + cruciō (“to torment”).

callum.e: Scottish surname, shortened from McCallum; also a variant of Calum.

stereotype.e: Borrowed from French stéréotype (adjective), equivalent to stereo- + type.

sustainable.e: Etymology tree English sustain Proto-Indo-European *-dʰlom Proto-Italic *-ðlom Proto-Italic *-ðlis Latin -bilis Latin -ābilis Old French -ablebor.

commissar.e: Borrowed from Russian комисса́р (komissár), from German Kommissar (“commissioner”), from Latin commissarius, from commissus, past participle of committō (“to commit, entrust to”). Doublet of commissary.

standpoint.e: From stand + point, a calque of German Standpunkt. Similar constructions used in other languages, such as Japanese 立場 (tachiba, literally “standing place”).

fruity.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewHg- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHgyéti Proto-Italic *frūgjōr Proto-Italic *frūjōr Latin fruor Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus Lati…

watcher.e: From Middle English wacchere, wachere, wacher, equivalent to watch + -er.

thereafter.e: From Middle English therafter, theraftir, þerefter, þerafter, þeræfter, from Old English þǣræfter (“after that; thereafter”), equivalent to there + after.

drifter.e: Etymology tree English drift Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

intimately.e: Etymology tree English intimate Proto-Indo-European *leyg-der. Proto-Germanic *līkąder.

wrapper.e: From Middle English wrappere, equivalent to wrap + -er.

alchemy.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew- Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥ Proto-Hellenic *-mə Ancient Greek -μᾰ (-mă) Ancient Greek χῠ́μᾰ (khŭ́mă) Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-i-eh₂…

antimatter.e: From anti- + matter. —A Holiday Dream", but not used in a modern sense until the 1940s.

saki.e: Compare French saki and Portuguese saki, ultimately probably from a Tupian name sagui, compare sagoin.

maki.e: From French maki, from Malagasy maky.

piers.e: A Middle English vernacular form of Peter, from Old French Piers, from Latin Petrus. Doublet of Pedro, Peter, and Boutros.

landon.e: Place names in England, from Old English lang (“long”) + dūn (“hill”).

curing.e: From Middle English curyng, curinge, equivalent to cure + -ing.

eject.e: From Middle French éjecter, from Latin ēiectus, perfect passive participle of ēiciō (“to throw out”), or from ēiectō, the frequentative form of the same verb, from ē-, combining form of ex (“out”), + iaciō (“to throw”).

banzai.e: e. “immortality”), from 萬 /万 (wàn, “10,000”) 歲 /岁 (suì, “year (of age)”). Compare Mandarin 萬歲／万岁 (wànsùi).

supplement.e: From Latin supplementum (“that which is added to supply a shortage”), from supplere (“to provide something”).

rollo.e: Latinization of the Old French equivalent of the English Rolf.

crucifix.e: From Middle English crucifix, from Old French crocefis (French crucifix), from Latin crucifixus.

czar.e: Etymology tree Latin Caesarbor. Proto-Germanic *kaisarazder. Proto-Slavic *cěsařь Old East Slavic цѣсарь (cěsarĭ) Old East Slavic цьсарь (cĭsarĭ) Russian царь (carʹ)bor. English czar See tsar.

seismic.e: Based on Ancient Greek σεισμός (seismós, “shaking, earthquake”) + -ic, equivalent to seismo- + -ic.

muppet.e: From Muppet, from the Muppets franchise

asphalt.e: From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”). Displaced native Old English eorþtyrewa (literally, "earth-tar").

tycoon.e: Borrowed from Japanese 大君 (“great lord, prince”), a title for the shōgun. Related to taipan, from Cantonese 大班 (daai⁶ baan¹). , RollerCoaster Tycoon).

aristocrat.e: From French aristocrate (“aristocrat”), attested once in the 16th century but recoined in the Revolutionary era, from aristocratie (“aristocracy”), from Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατία (aris…

epilepsy.e: Since 16th century; borrowed from French épilepsie, from Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψίᾱ (epilēpsíā), from ἐπιλαμβάνω (epilambánō, “to seize”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

shakily.e: Etymology tree English shaky Middle English -ly English -ly English shakily From shaky + -ly.

wakey.e: Etymology tree English wake Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English wakey From wake + -y (diminutive suffix).

poacher.e: Etymology tree English poach Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

balm.e: Inherited from Middle English bawme, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Middle French baume, from Old French basme, from Latin balsamum, itself from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon). Spelling modified 16th c.

nagasaki.e: Borrowed from Japanese 長崎(ながさき) (Nagasaki).

cooker.e: From cook + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix) (apple; one who is cooked).

georgetown.e: From George + town, both capitals were named after King George III of the United Kingdom.

mach.e: * As a Polish, Czech, Slovak, Ukrainian, and Lower Sorbian surname, from pet forms produced by truncation of personal names beginning with Ma- such as Matej, Martin, or Maciej, and the addition of the Slavic suffix -ch.

yippee.e: Of imitative origin. Perhaps an extension and modification of hip (interjection). Compare Dutch joepie (“yippee”).

steamer.e: From steam + -er. 2) is apparently named for its resemblance to a paddle steamer when swimming rapidly.

flunk.e: Alteration of funk, or perhaps a blend of flinch + funk.

sabina.e: Name of early saints, Latin Sabīna, feminine of the Roman cognomen Sabīnus (“a Sabine”), from an ancient tribe from Italy.

nesting.e: From Old Norse nes + þing, the ting (assembly) at the ness; there are a few nesses in the area.

blackberry.e: Etymology tree Old English blæcberġe Middle English blakberie English blackberry From Middle English blakberie, blakeberie (“brambleberry”), from Old English blacu berġe, blæcberġe (attested in plural blaca berġan), equ…

fiercely.e: From Middle English fersly; equivalent to fierce + -ly.

impound.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Italic *n̥- Latin in-bor. Middle English in- English im- English pound English impound From im- + pound.

bengal.e: Borrowed from Portuguese Bengala, from Classical Persian بَنْگَالَه (bangāla), from Middle Bengali বাঙ্গালা (baṅgala), said to be from the Vanga Kingdom, of uncertain ultimate origin.

cache.e: From French cache (as used by French Canadian trappers to mean “hiding place for stores”), from the verb cacher (“to hide”).

crème.e: Unadapted borrowing from French crème. Doublet of cream and crema.

rhine.e: From Middle English Rine, Ryne, from Old English Rīn (“the Rhine”), from Middle High German and Old High German Rīn, from Proto-West Germanic *Rīn, from Proto-Germanic *Rīnaz, from Gaulish Rēnos, from a Pre-Celtic or Pr…

consequently.e: From Middle English consequentely, consequentliche, consequently; equivalent to consequent + -ly.

shim.e: Unknown; from Kent. Originally a piece of iron attached to a plow; sense of “thin piece of wood” from 1723, sense of “thin piece of material used for alignment or support” from 1860.

rosewood.e: A compound of rose + wood, originally so named because of the rose-scented aromatic oil derived from it; applied in later senses on account of these woods’ predominantly reddish-brown colour.

larva.e: From Latin larva (“disembodied spirit, ghost, goblin”).

yeti.e: ya', “dirt, rust, slate”) and དྲེད (dred, “bear”). Attested since 1937.

jeanie.e: v. Doublet of Ivanka, Jan, Janelle, Janet, Janey, Janine, Jeanette, Jeannette, Jeannine, Jen, Jenna, Jenny, Jessie, Jo, Jody, Juanita, Shanae, Sinead, and Vanna.

aphrodite.e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀφροδίτη (Aphrodítē) (see it for more).

snuggle.e: Etymology tree English snug Proto-Germanic *-lōną Old English -lian Middle English -len English -le English snuggle From snug + -le (frequentative suffix).

pre.e: From Latin prae (“in front of”); see pre-.

nassau.e: Borrowed from German Nassau, from German nass (“wet”). The Bahamian city is named after the German one.

hombre.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dʰeǵʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-ōm Proto-Indo-European *dʰéǵʰōm Proto-Indo-European *-ō Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰmṓ Proto-Italic *hemō Latin hemō Latin homō Latin hominem Old Spanish omne…

nook.e: From Middle English noke, nok (“nook, corner, angle”), of uncertain origin.

cyclone.e: Coined by English scientist and merchant captain Henry Piddington, probably in the 1840s, and based on some term in Ancient Greek.

zheng.e: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of Mandarin 鄭 /郑 (Zhèng).

lovingly.e: Etymology tree English loving Middle English -ly English -ly English lovingly From loving + -ly.

colonist.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *kʷélh₁eti Proto-Italic *kʷelō Latin colō Latin colōnus Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old L…

unwise.e: From Middle English unwis, from Old English unwīs (“unwise, foolish, ignorant, uninformed, insane”), equivalent to un- + wise.

affliction.e: From Middle English affliction, affliccioun, from Old French afliction, borrowed from Latin afflīctiōnem (“pain, suffering, torment”), from Latin afflīctō (“to damage, harass, torment”), from ad- + flīctus, past partici…

dow.e: From Middle English douen, from Old English dugan, from Proto-West Germanic *dugan, from Proto-Germanic *duganą.

hooch.e: Abbreviation of hoochinoo, name of a specific liquor, from Tlingit Xutsnoowú Ḵwáan, the group that produced it, from Hutsnuwu (“grizzly bear fort”), the name of the village on Admiralty Island in which they lived.

laceration.e: From Latin lacerātiō, first attested in 1598. By surface analysis, lacerate + -tion. Compare lacerate.

tasteless.e: Etymology tree English taste Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *lewHs-der.

deirdre.e: From Irish Deirdre, from Old Irish Derdriu.

welch.e: Alternative form of welsh, from Welsh.

unbreakable.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *né Proto-Indo-European *n̥- Proto-Germanic *un- Proto-West Germanic *un- Old English un- Middle English un- English un- Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Ind…

carnal.e: From Middle English carnal, from Old French charnel, from Late Latin carnālis (“fleshy”), from oblique stem of Latin carō, carnis (“meat, flesh”) + -ālis (whence -al).

generic.e: From Middle French générique, from Latin genus (“genus, kind”) + -ic.

sentinel.e: First attested in the 1570s from Middle French sentinelle (“watch or guard kept by a soldier”), from Old Italian sentinella, probably from sentina + -ella, from sentire (“perceive, watch, hear”), from sentiō (“feel, per…

yelping.e: From Middle English yelpynge, from Old English ġilping; equivalent to yelp + -ing.

renault.e: Borrowed from French Renault, itself derived from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz. Doublet of Reynold.

efficiently.e: Etymology tree English efficient Middle English -ly English -ly English efficiently From efficient + -ly.

wilhelmina.e: Borrowed from German Wilhelmina, equivalent to Wilhelm + -ina.

hashtag.e: From earlier hash tag, from hash (sign) + tag. The hash sign # was initially proposed as tag hash by Chris Messina to create groups on Twitter, modeled after the IRC channel prefix.

emphasize.e: Latin, from Ancient Greek – see emphasis. By surface analysis, emphasis + -ize.

scat.e: From Middle English scet, schat, from Old English sċeatt (“property, goods”) and Old Norse skattr (“wealth, treaure”); both from Proto-Germanic *skattaz (“cattle, kine, wealth”), from Proto-Indo-European *skatn-, *skat-…

chardonnay.e: Borrowed from French chardonnay, believed to be named after the village of Chardonnay in the Mâconnais region of France, where Pouilly-Fuissé is currently produced; it is possible that the variety was first bred there

nigeria.e: Etymology tree Tuareg n'igherren? ▲ Latin nigerinflu. French Nigerbor. English Niger Proto-Indo-European *-(i)yós Proto-Italic *-ijos Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -iader.

deactivate.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der.

regrettable.e: Etymology tree Proto-Italic *wre- Latin re-der. Old French re- Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁d-der. Proto-Germanic *grētaną Frankish *grātander. Old French *greter Old French regreterbor.

evasion.e: From Middle French évasion, from Late Latin evasionem (accusative of evasio).

clementine.e: Etymology tree French Clément Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos Proto-Italic *-īnos Latin -īnus French -in Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂ Proto-Italic *-ā Latin -am Old French -e…

overworked.e: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *úp Proto-Indo-European *-er Proto-Indo-European *upér Proto-Germanic *uber Old English ofer- Middle English over- English over- English worked English overworked From over- + worked.

waterproof.e: From water + -proof. Compare West Frisian wetterproef (“waterproof”), Dutch waterproef (“waterproof”).

alamo.e: From Spanish álamo. Doublet of elm.

salome.e: From Ancient Greek Σαλώμη (Salṓmē), from Hebrew שְׁלוֹמִית (sh'lomít) (belonging to the same root as שָׁלוֹם (shalóm, “peace”)).

halibut.e: From Middle English halibut, equivalent to holy + butt (“flatfish”), since the fish was often eaten on holy days.

communicator.e: From communicate + -or, after Latin commūnicātor (“partner, sharer, participant”); compare Middle French communicateur (“sharer, participant”).

phi.e: From Late Latin phi, from Ancient Greek φεῖ (pheî).

garnish.e: From Middle English garnysshen, from Old French garniss-, stem of certain forms of the verb garnir, guarnir, warnir (“to provide, furnish, avert, defend, warn, fortify, garnish”), from a conflation of Old Frankish *warn…

spruce.e: From Middle English Spruce, an alteration of Pruce (“Prussia”), from Medieval Latin, from a Baltic language, probably Old Prussian; for more, see Prussia.

leper.e: ], from Latin leprae, lepra, from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra).

ponder.e: From Middle English ponderen, from Old French ponderer (“to weigh, balance, ponder”) from Latin ponderāre (“to weigh, ponder”), from pondus (“weight”), from pendere (“to weigh”); see pendent and pound.

technicality.e: Etymology tree English technical Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-ts Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts Latin -itāsder. Old French -itebor.

vindictive.e: From Latin vindicta (“vengeance”) + -ive. Contrast Latin vindicātīvus.

twit.e: PIE word *h₂éd The verb is an apheretic form of atwite (“(obsolete) to blame, reproach”), from Middle English atwiten (“to attribute (something) to someone; to blame (something) on someone; to accuse or charge (someone)…

lutz.e: From the surname of Austrian skater Alois Lutz, who invented the jump.

waldorf.e: Ultimately from the German town name, Walldorf.

shogunate.e: Etymology tree English shogun Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Italic *-tus Latin -tus, -tūs Latin -ātusder. English -ate English shogunate From shogun + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

mural.e: Borrowed from French mural, from Latin muralis, from murus (“wall”).

enlarge.e: From Middle English enlargen, from Old French enlargier, enlargir. By surface analysis, en- + large.

contender.e: Etymology tree English contend Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor.

orpheus.e: From Ancient Greek Ὀρφεύς (Orpheús), built from an uncertain root with the -εύς (-eús) suffix. Perhaps root-cognate to Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “orphan”).

hammock.e: Borrowed from Spanish hamaca, from Taíno *hamaka (compare Lokono hamaka, Wayuu jama'a), from Proto-Arawak *maka.

whistler.e: From Middle English whisteler, whistlar, whystelare, from Old English hwistlere (“a player on a flute; a piper”), equivalent to whistle + -er.

tehran.e: A diacriticless transliteration of Iranian Persian تِهران (tehrân), from Classical Persian تَهران (tahrān). See there for more.

pasadena.e: The place name in California is claimed to be from an Ojibwe word meaning “crown of the valley”. The town in Newfoundland is named after a farm which was named in turn for the city in California.

tig.e: Dialectal variant of tick, from Middle English ticken, tiken. More at tick.

sos.e: From interpretation of the signal (· · · — — — · · ·), chosen merely as a sequence that is easy to recall and transmit, as normal Morse letters.

edwina.e: Female form of Edwin from Old English, equivalent to Edwin + -a.

starry.e: From Middle English sterry, equivalent to star + -y.

savoy.e: From French Savoy , Savoie, from the Roman name, Late Latin Sapaudia. See sappinus (“type of fir”).

fahrenheit.e: From German Fahrenheit, named after Prussian scientist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit.

chaste.e: From Middle English chaste, from Old French chaste (“morally pure”), from Latin castus (“pure”).
s: having or providing no sexual knowledge or experience

buttercup.e: From butter + cup. Both sense 1 and 2 are from the flowers' association with butter, from their yellow colour.

stoner.e: From Middle English stoner, stonere, stonare, staner, equivalent to stone + -er (agent noun suffix) or -er (measurement suffix).

hitter.e: From hit + -er (agent noun suffix) or -er (measurement suffix).

anonymity.e: From Latin anonymus or its etymon Ancient Greek ἀνώνυμος (anṓnumos, “anonymous”) + -ity. Compare French anonymité.

dodd.e: Uncertain, but possibly from any of the following: # Old English personal names Dodd(a), Dudd(a) # The Proto-Germanic root *dudd-/*dodd- (“rounded”), denoting a rounded, lumpish man, or a stupid person.

insecurity.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnsēcūritās. By surface analysis, insecure + -ity.
